AP Physics 1 | Georgia Standards of Excellence College Board CED Topic: KIN-1 through KIN-5

1.1

Position, Displacement, and Distance

Before we can describe how objects move, we must first establish precise language for where they are and how far they have traveled. Physics distinguishes carefully between two fundamentally different ideas: displacement and distance. This distinction matters enormously because all of the laws governing motion are written in terms of vector quantities, and position is the most fundamental vector in mechanics.

Position (x or r) is the location of an object measured from a chosen reference point called the origin. Because position has both magnitude and direction, it is a vector. You are free to choose any origin and any positive direction — the physics will work out the same — but you must commit to your choice and be consistent throughout a problem.

Displacement (Δx) is the change in position: Δx = x_f − x_i. It is also a vector. Crucially, displacement depends only on where you started and where you ended, not on the route taken. A hiker who walks 5 km north and then 3 km south has a displacement of 2 km north, regardless of the winding path.

Distance (d) is the total length of path traveled — a scalar that accumulates all movement regardless of direction. It is always non-negative. The same hiker walked a total distance of 8 km, even though her displacement was only 2 km.

Why the distinction matters: When we compute energy stored in a spring or work done by friction, it is the distance that matters. When we compute the net effect of a force or the final velocity, it is displacement. Confusing the two is one of the most common errors in AP Physics.

Δx = x_f − x_i              [meters, m]
d  = |seg₁| + |seg₂| + ...  [meters, m, always ≥ 0]

Example: Car goes 100 m east (+), then 40 m west (−)
  Displacement:  Δx = +100 − 40 = +60 m (east)
  Distance:      d  = 100 + 40  = 140 m
SymbolQuantityTypeSI Unit

x_ffinal positionvectorm

1.2

Velocity and Speed

Knowing an object's position tells us where it is. Knowing how quickly that position changes tells us about its velocity. Velocity is the rate of change of position with respect to time — it is, fundamentally, a derivative in the calculus sense, though we can approach it algebraically first.

Average velocity is defined as the total displacement divided by the total time elapsed: v_avg = Δx / Δt. Because displacement is a vector, average velocity is also a vector. It tells you the net rate at which position changed, but nothing about the details of the journey. A car that completes a circular track in 60 seconds has zero average velocity, even though it was moving the whole time.

Average speed is the total distance traveled divided by time: s_avg = d / Δt. Speed is a scalar — it is never negative. For the circular track car, the average speed is the circumference divided by 60 seconds.

Instantaneous velocity is the limit of average velocity as the time interval Δt shrinks toward zero: v(t) = dx/dt. Graphically, it is the slope of the tangent line to the position-versus-time (x-t) graph at any given moment. When you look at your car's speedometer, it displays instantaneous speed — the magnitude of instantaneous velocity.

Reading x-t graphs: A steeper positive slope means faster motion in the positive direction. A negative slope means motion in the negative direction. A horizontal line means the object is at rest. A curve means the velocity is changing — acceleration is present.

v_avg = Δx/Δt = (x_f − x_i)/(t_f − t_i)  [m/s, vector]
s_avg = total distance / total time         [m/s, scalar]
v(t)  = lim(Δt→0) Δx/Δt = dx/dt           [m/s, calculus form]

Graph rule: slope of x-t graph = instantaneous velocity
1.3

Acceleration

Just as velocity describes how quickly position changes, acceleration describes how quickly velocity changes. Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity with respect to time: a = Δv/Δt (average) or a = dv/dt (instantaneous). It is a vector, with both magnitude and direction.

One of the most persistent conceptual pitfalls is equating "positive acceleration" with "speeding up." This is wrong. Whether an object speeds up or slows down depends on the relative directions of velocity and acceleration. When they point in the same direction, the object speeds up. When they point in opposite directions, the object slows down. A ball thrown upward has a downward acceleration due to gravity the entire time — while it rises (velocity upward, acceleration downward), it decelerates; while it falls (both downward), it accelerates.

For AP Physics C students, acceleration also equals the second derivative of position: a(t) = dv/dt = d²x/dt². This allows us to move fluidly between position, velocity, and acceleration using calculus.

Key graph relationships: The slope of the v-t graph gives instantaneous acceleration. The area under the v-t graph (∫v dt) gives the displacement. These derivative-integral pairs are fundamental throughout all of physics.

a_avg = Δv/Δt = (v_f − v_i)/(t_f − t_i)  [m/s², vector]
a(t)  = dv/dt = d²x/dt²                    [calculus form]

Graph rules:
  Slope of v-t graph = instantaneous acceleration
  Area under v-t graph = displacement (Δx = ∫v dt)

Car braking going right+−Slowing down →

1.4

Kinematic Equations for Constant Acceleration

When acceleration is constant — unchanging in both magnitude and direction — we can derive four powerful algebraic equations that connect position, velocity, acceleration, and time. These are often called the SUVAT equations or simply the kinematic equations. They are the workhorses of introductory mechanics.

Each equation contains four of the five kinematic variables (x₀, x, v₀, v, a, t — five variables, but one is always known or zero). The strategy for any constant-acceleration problem: (1) identify which variables are given and which is unknown, (2) select the equation that contains exactly those variables, (3) solve algebraically before substituting numbers, and (4) check units and sign.

Equation 1 — v = v₀ + at: Directly relates velocity to time. Use when time is known and final velocity sought, or vice versa.

Equation 2 — Δx = v₀t + ½at²: Gives displacement as a function of time. The ½at² term is the extra displacement due to acceleration beyond uniform motion.

Equation 3 — v² = v₀² + 2aΔx: The "timeless" equation — useful when time is neither given nor wanted. It directly connects speed to displacement through acceleration.

Equation 4 — Δx = ½(v₀ + v)t: Uses the average of initial and final velocity. Valid only for constant acceleration, where the v-t graph is linear.

Free fall as a special case: Near Earth's surface, gravity provides a constant downward acceleration of g = 9.8 m/s². Taking upward as positive, a = −g = −9.8 m/s² for any freely falling object. At the peak of a trajectory, velocity is exactly zero — but acceleration is most definitely NOT zero. The ball is still being pulled downward by gravity; it just happens to have zero velocity at that one instant.

THE FOUR KINEMATIC EQUATIONS (constant acceleration only):
  (1)  v   = v₀ + at           [missing: Δx]
  (2)  Δx  = v₀t + ½at²        [missing: v]
  (3)  v²  = v₀² + 2aΔx        [missing: t]
  (4)  Δx  = ½(v₀ + v)t        [missing: a]

Free Fall: a = −g = −9.8 m/s² (taking up as positive)
Peak of trajectory: v = 0, but a = −9.8 m/s² ≠ 0
EquationVariables KnownVariable Found
v = v₀ + atv₀, a, tv (no position needed)
Δx = v₀t + ½at²v₀, a, tΔx (no final v needed)
v² = v₀² + 2aΔxv₀, v, Δxa or any — no time!
Δx = ½(v₀+v)tv₀, v, tΔx (no a needed)
1.5

Two-Dimensional Kinematics and Projectile Motion

Most real-world motion occurs in two or three dimensions. The key insight that makes 2D kinematics tractable is the principle of independence of motion: the horizontal and vertical components of motion are completely independent of each other. A force acting in the x-direction changes only the x-component of velocity; it has zero effect on the y-component. This is an exact mathematical consequence of Newton's Second Law applied to vector quantities — not an approximation.

Projectile motion is the canonical 2D kinematics problem. A projectile is any object that, once launched, experiences only the force of gravity (we neglect air resistance unless told otherwise). The horizontal motion is uniform (constant velocity — no horizontal force), while the vertical motion is free fall (constant downward acceleration g).

Setting up a projectile problem: Decompose the initial velocity into components: v₀ₓ = v₀ cosθ and v₀ᵧ = v₀ sinθ where θ is measured from the horizontal. Treat x and y as two separate 1D problems, linked only by the shared time variable t.

Key symmetry results: The maximum range occurs at θ = 45° (sin2θ is maximized). Complementary launch angles (like 30° and 60°) produce equal ranges on level ground. The time of flight is determined solely by the vertical motion — the initial vertical velocity and g. The horizontal range is then simply R = vₓ × T.

COMPONENT DECOMPOSITION:
  v₀ₓ = v₀ cosθ    v₀ᵧ = v₀ sinθ

HORIZONTAL (aₓ = 0):
  x(t) = x₀ + v₀ₓ · t
  vₓ = v₀ₓ = constant throughout flight

VERTICAL (aᵧ = −g, taking up as positive):
  y(t) = y₀ + v₀ᵧt − ½gt²
  vᵧ(t) = v₀ᵧ − gt
  vᵧ² = v₀ᵧ² − 2g(Δy)

LEVEL-GROUND LAUNCH RESULTS (y₀ = y_f = 0):
  Time of flight:  T = 2v₀ sinθ / g
  Range:           R = v₀² sin(2θ) / g   (max at θ = 45°)
  Max height:      H = v₀² sin²θ / (2g)
1.1

Position-Time Graph (x-t): Reading Motion

The x-t graph is the most fundamental kinematic tool. The slope at any point equals the instantaneous velocity. Positive slope = rightward motion; negative slope = leftward; zero slope = at rest; curved sections = changing velocity (acceleration present).

Text version of this diagram
x (m)
│         C (slope = 0, at rest)
│        /─────────│       /           │      / B           \ D (negative slope = moving left)
│     /               ──────
│    / A (positive slope = moving right)
│   /
└──────────────────────────── t (s)

Segment A: slope > 0 → moving in +x direction, constant v
Segment B: increasing slope → speeding up (+acceleration)
Segment C: slope = 0 → momentarily at rest (v = 0)
Segment D: slope < 0 → moving in −x direction
1.2

Velocity-Time Graph (v-t): Area = Displacement

On a v-t graph: slope = acceleration; area under curve = displacement. Areas above the axis are positive displacement; below are negative. This is the graphical meaning of Δx = ∫v dt.

Text version of this diagram
v (m/s)
│    ╱────╲
│   ╱  (+) ╲         Area under curve = net displacement
│  ╱         ╲
│ ╱            ╲
──╱──────────────╲──────── t (s)
                  ╲  (−)
                   ╲────

Slope = Δv/Δt = acceleration [m/s²]
Area above axis → positive displacement (+x)
Area below axis → negative displacement (−x)
Slope = 0 → constant velocity (a = 0)
1.3

Projectile Motion: Independent Components

Horizontal and vertical motions are completely independent. Horizontal velocity stays constant; vertical velocity changes at rate g. Both share the same time variable — the link between the two equations.

Text version of this diagram
y (m)      ● peak: vx = v₀cosθ, vy = 0
          /          /   \         vx constant throughout
        / ↗↑  \ ↘
       /        \ ↓
  ●──              ──●
launch                landing

Horizontal: x = v₀cosθ · t     (no force, uniform motion)
Vertical:   y = v₀sinθ · t − ½gt²  (free fall with initial vy)
Shared:     same t in both equations

Range R = v₀² sin(2θ)/g   Maximum at θ = 45°
Example 1.1

Displacement vs. Distance

Qualitative Reasoning

Question: A jogger runs 400 m north, then 150 m south. Find (a) total distance and (b) displacement.

Show solution

Solution:

(a) Distance = sum of all path lengths
    d = 400 m + 150 m = 550 m

(b) Displacement = final position − initial position
    Take north as positive (+)
    Δx = (+400 m) + (−150 m) = +250 m (north)

Answer: distance = 550 m; displacement = 250 m north
Example 1.2

Average Velocity Calculation

Algebraic Calculation

Question: A car travels from x₁ = 10 m to x₂ = 85 m in 5.0 s. What is the average velocity?

Show solution

Solution:

v_avg = Δx / Δt
v_avg = (x₂ − x₁) / (t₂ − t₁)
v_avg = (85 m − 10 m) / (5.0 s − 0 s)
v_avg = 75 m / 5.0 s
v_avg = 15 m/s (in +x direction)
Example 1.3

Kinematic Equation: Finding Final Velocity

Algebraic Calculation

Question: A car starts from rest and accelerates at 3.0 m/s² for 8.0 s. What is its final velocity?

Show solution

Solution:

Known: v₀ = 0, a = 3.0 m/s², t = 8.0 s
Unknown: v

Use: v = v₀ + at
     v = 0 + (3.0 m/s²)(8.0 s)
     v = 24 m/s
Example 1.4

Stopping Distance

Algebraic Calculation

Question: A car moving at 30 m/s brakes with deceleration 6.0 m/s². How far does it travel before stopping?

Show solution

Solution:

Known: v₀ = 30 m/s, v = 0, a = −6.0 m/s²
Unknown: Δx

Use: v² = v₀² + 2aΔx
     0 = (30)² + 2(−6.0)(Δx)
     0 = 900 − 12Δx
     12Δx = 900
     Δx = 75 m
Example 1.5

Time to Reach Maximum Height

Algebraic Calculation

Question: A ball is thrown upward at 20 m/s from ground level. Find (a) time to reach max height, (b) max height, (c) total air time.

Show solution

Solution:

Take up as positive. a = −9.8 m/s²

(a) At max height, v = 0
    v = v₀ + at
    0 = 20 + (−9.8)t
    t = 20/9.8 = 2.04 s

(b) H = v₀t + ½at²
    H = 20(2.04) + ½(−9.8)(2.04)²
    H = 40.8 − 20.4 = 20.4 m

    Check with: v² = v₀² + 2aΔy
    0 = 400 + 2(−9.8)H
    H = 400/19.6 = 20.4 m ✓

(c) By symmetry: total time = 2 × t_up = 2 × 2.04 = 4.08 s
Example 1.6

Graph Interpretation: Displacement from v-t

Graph Interpretation

Question: A v-t graph shows velocity constant at 4 m/s from t=0 to t=3 s, then linearly decreasing to 0 at t=5 s. Find total displacement.

Show solution

Solution:

Displacement = area under v-t graph

Rectangle (0 to 3 s):
  A₁ = base × height = 3 s × 4 m/s = 12 m

Triangle (3 to 5 s):
  A₂ = ½ × base × height = ½ × 2 s × 4 m/s = 4 m

Total displacement = A₁ + A₂ = 12 + 4 = 16 m
Example 1.7

Calculus: Velocity from Position Function

Calculus Derivation

Question: The position of a particle is given by x(t) = 3t³ − 5t² + 2t − 1 (meters). Find (a) velocity at t=2 s, (b) acceleration at t=2 s.

Show solution

Solution:

(a) v(t) = dx/dt = d/dt[3t³ − 5t² + 2t − 1]
           = 9t² − 10t + 2

    v(2) = 9(4) − 10(2) + 2 = 36 − 20 + 2 = 18 m/s

(b) a(t) = dv/dt = d/dt[9t² − 10t + 2]
           = 18t − 10

    a(2) = 18(2) − 10 = 36 − 10 = 26 m/s²
Example 1.8

Calculus: Position from Acceleration

Calculus Derivation

Question: A particle starts at x=2 m with v₀=3 m/s and has acceleration a(t) = 6t m/s². Find x(t).

Show solution

Solution:

Step 1: Integrate acceleration to get velocity
  v(t) = ∫a dt = ∫6t dt = 3t² + C₁
  Apply initial condition: v(0) = 3 m/s
  3 = 3(0)² + C₁  →  C₁ = 3
  v(t) = 3t² + 3

Step 2: Integrate velocity to get position
  x(t) = ∫v dt = ∫(3t² + 3) dt = t³ + 3t + C₂
  Apply initial condition: x(0) = 2 m
  2 = 0 + 0 + C₂  →  C₂ = 2
  x(t) = t³ + 3t + 2
Example 1.9

Projectile: Range Calculation

Algebraic Calculation

Question: A ball is launched at 25 m/s at 35° above horizontal from ground level. Find (a) horizontal range, (b) max height. (g = 9.8 m/s²)

Show solution

Solution:

Step 1: Decompose initial velocity
  v₀ₓ = 25 cos35° = 25(0.819) = 20.5 m/s
  v₀ᵧ = 25 sin35° = 25(0.574) = 14.3 m/s

(a) Time of flight:
    vᵧ = v₀ᵧ − gt = 0 at peak
    t_peak = 14.3/9.8 = 1.46 s
    T_total = 2(1.46) = 2.92 s

    Range R = v₀ₓ × T = 20.5 × 2.92 = 59.8 m

    Check with formula: R = v₀²sin(2θ)/g
    R = (25)²sin(70°)/9.8 = 625(0.940)/9.8 = 60.0 m ✓

(b) Max height:
    H = v₀ᵧ²/(2g) = (14.3)²/(2×9.8) = 204.5/19.6 = 10.4 m
Example 1.10

Projectile: Cliff Launch

Algebraic Calculation

Question: A projectile is launched horizontally at 15 m/s from a cliff 45 m high. Find (a) time to hit ground, (b) horizontal distance, (c) speed just before impact.

Show solution

Solution:

Setup: v₀ₓ = 15 m/s, v₀ᵧ = 0 (horizontal launch)
       y₀ = 45 m, y = 0 (taking down as positive for convenience)

(a) Vertical: y = ½gt²
    45 = ½(9.8)t²
    t² = 90/9.8 = 9.18
    t = 3.03 s

(b) Horizontal: x = v₀ₓ · t = 15 × 3.03 = 45.5 m

(c) At impact:
    vₓ = 15 m/s (unchanged)
    vᵧ = gt = 9.8 × 3.03 = 29.7 m/s (downward)
    
    v = √(vₓ² + vᵧ²) = √(225 + 882) = √1107 = 33.3 m/s
Example 1.11

Relative Motion

Algebraic Calculation

Question: Train A moves east at 60 m/s. Train B moves west at 40 m/s. They are 500 m apart. When do they meet?

Show solution

Solution:

Take east as positive.
v_A = +60 m/s, v_B = −40 m/s

Relative velocity of approach = 60 + 40 = 100 m/s
(they move toward each other)

Time to meet: t = separation / relative speed
t = 500 m / 100 m/s = 5.0 s

Position of A: x_A = 60(5) = 300 m from A's start
Position of B: x_B = 500 − 40(5) = 500 − 200 = 300 m ✓
Example 1.12

Acceleration from Graph

Graph Interpretation

Question: A v-t graph shows v = 2 m/s at t=1 s and v = 14 m/s at t=4 s. Find acceleration and displacement from t=1 to t=4 s.

Show solution

Solution:

Acceleration = slope of v-t graph
a = Δv/Δt = (14 − 2)/(4 − 1) = 12/3 = 4 m/s²

Displacement = area under v-t graph (trapezoid):
Δx = ½(v₁ + v₂) × Δt = ½(2 + 14) × 3 = ½ × 16 × 3 = 24 m

Verify with equation: Δx = v₀t + ½at²
Δx = 2(3) + ½(4)(9) = 6 + 18 = 24 m ✓
Example 1.13

Two Objects Meeting

Algebraic Calculation

Question: Object A starts at x=0 and moves at constant 5 m/s. Object B starts at x=60 m and moves at −3 m/s (toward A). When and where do they meet?

Show solution

Solution:

Position equations:
  x_A(t) = 0 + 5t = 5t
  x_B(t) = 60 + (−3)t = 60 − 3t

Set equal to find meeting time:
  5t = 60 − 3t
  8t = 60
  t = 7.5 s

Meeting position:
  x = 5(7.5) = 37.5 m from origin
  Check: x_B = 60 − 3(7.5) = 60 − 22.5 = 37.5 m ✓
Example 1.14

Free Fall with Initial Downward Velocity

Algebraic Calculation

Question: An object is thrown downward at 8 m/s from 50 m height. Find (a) time to hit ground, (b) impact speed.

Show solution

Solution:

Take downward as positive. a = +9.8 m/s², v₀ = +8 m/s

(a) y = v₀t + ½at²
    50 = 8t + ½(9.8)t²
    4.9t² + 8t − 50 = 0
    
    Quadratic formula: t = [−8 ± √(64 + 4×4.9×50)] / (2×4.9)
    t = [−8 ± √(64 + 980)] / 9.8
    t = [−8 ± √1044] / 9.8
    t = [−8 ± 32.3] / 9.8
    
    Taking positive root: t = (−8 + 32.3)/9.8 = 24.3/9.8 = 2.48 s

(b) v = v₀ + at = 8 + 9.8(2.48) = 8 + 24.3 = 32.3 m/s
Example 1.15

Projectile: Angle for Maximum Range

Qualitative Reasoning + Algebraic

Question: Prove that maximum range occurs at θ = 45°. For v₀ = 20 m/s, calculate range at 30°, 45°, and 60°.

Show solution

Solution:

Range formula: R = v₀²sin(2θ)/g

For maximum R: sin(2θ) must equal 1
sin(2θ) = 1  →  2θ = 90°  →  θ = 45° ✓

Calculations (v₀=20, g=9.8):
  R_max = (20)²/9.8 = 400/9.8 = 40.8 m (at θ=45°)

  θ=30°: R = (400)sin(60°)/9.8 = 400(0.866)/9.8 = 35.3 m
  θ=45°: R = (400)sin(90°)/9.8 = 400(1.00)/9.8 = 40.8 m ✓
  θ=60°: R = (400)sin(120°)/9.8 = 400(0.866)/9.8 = 35.3 m

Note: 30° and 60° give same range (complementary angles property)
Example 1.16

Non-Uniform Acceleration (AP-C Level)

Calculus Derivation

Question: A particle has acceleration a(t) = (4 − 2t) m/s². At t=0: v₀=0, x₀=

  1. Find: (a) when it stops, (b) max displacement.
Show solution

Solution:

(a) v(t) = ∫a dt = ∫(4 − 2t) dt = 4t − t² + C
    v(0) = 0  →  C = 0
    v(t) = 4t − t²

    Stops when v = 0:
    4t − t² = 0  →  t(4 − t) = 0
    t = 0 (start) or t = 4 s

(b) x(t) = ∫v dt = ∫(4t − t²) dt = 2t² − t³/3 + C
    x(0) = 0  →  C = 0
    x(t) = 2t² − t³/3

    Max displacement at t = 4 s:
    x(4) = 2(16) − (64)/3 = 32 − 21.3 = 10.7 m
Example 1.17

Projectile: Hitting a Moving Target (FRQ Style)

Algebraic Calculation (Multi-part)

Question: A cannon fires at 50 m/s at 37° above horizontal (sin37°=0.6, cos37°=0.8). A target is 120 m away horizontally at ground level. (a) Does the projectile hit the target? (b) If not, what angle is needed?

Show solution

Solution:

(a) Check if range = 120 m
    R = v₀²sin(2θ)/g = (2500)sin(74°)/9.8
    R = 2500(0.961)/9.8 = 245 m ≠ 120 m
    Does NOT hit at 37°.

(b) Need: R = 120 m
    120 = (2500)sin(2θ)/9.8
    sin(2θ) = 120(9.8)/2500 = 1176/2500 = 0.470
    2θ = 28.0° or 152°
    θ = 14.0° or 76.0°
    
    Two angles work (complementary angle property).
    Use θ = 14.0° for low trajectory or 76.0° for high trajectory.
Example 1.18

Instantaneous vs. Average Velocity

Qualitative Reasoning

Question: Position is x(t) = t² − 4t + 3 (meters). (a) Find avg velocity 0→3 s. (b) Find instantaneous velocity at t=1, t=2, t=3 s. (c) When is the object momentarily at rest?

Show solution

Solution:

(a) x(0) = 0 − 0 + 3 = 3 m
    x(3) = 9 − 12 + 3 = 0 m
    v_avg = (0 − 3)/3 = −1 m/s

(b) v(t) = dx/dt = 2t − 4
    v(1) = 2(1) − 4 = −2 m/s
    v(2) = 2(2) − 4 = 0 m/s
    v(3) = 2(3) − 4 = +2 m/s

(c) At rest: v(t) = 0
    2t − 4 = 0  →  t = 2 s
    Position: x(2) = 4 − 8 + 3 = −1 m
Example 1.19

Vector Addition of Velocities

Algebraic Calculation

Question: A boat heads east at 4 m/s. River current flows north at 3 m/s. Find (a) resultant velocity, (b) angle from east, (c) time to cross 80 m wide river.

Show solution

Solution:

(a) v = √(vₓ² + vᵧ²) = √(16 + 9) = √25 = 5 m/s

(b) θ = arctan(vᵧ/vₓ) = arctan(3/4) = 36.9° north of east

(c) To cross 80 m wide river (crossing in x-direction):
    Time depends only on component perpendicular to shore.
    
    If river flows north and boat heads east:
    The east component (4 m/s) carries boat across 80 m river
    t = 80/4 = 20 s
    
    Boat drifts north: d = vₙ × t = 3 × 20 = 60 m downstream
Example 1.20

AP FRQ: Complete Projectile Analysis

Free Response Question (Multi-part)

Question: A ball is launched from the edge of a table (height H = 1.2 m) with initial horizontal velocity v₀. It lands 2.4 m from the base of the table. (a) Find the time of flight. (b) Find v₀. (c) Find the velocity (magnitude and direction) just before impact. (d) Sketch the trajectory labeling key quantities.

Show solution

Solution:

(a) Vertical drop: H = ½gt²
    1.2 = ½(9.8)t²
    t² = 2.4/9.8 = 0.245
    t = 0.495 s ≈ 0.50 s

(b) Horizontal: x = v₀t
    2.4 = v₀(0.495)
    v₀ = 2.4/0.495 = 4.85 m/s

(c) At impact:
    vₓ = v₀ = 4.85 m/s (unchanged)
    vᵧ = gt = 9.8(0.495) = 4.85 m/s (downward)
    
    |v| = √(4.85² + 4.85²) = 4.85√2 = 6.86 m/s
    θ = arctan(vᵧ/vₓ) = arctan(1) = 45° below horizontal

(d) Sketch description:
    - Horizontal launch arrow v₀ at table edge
    - Parabolic curve downward to landing point
    - Label: H = 1.2 m (vertical), R = 2.4 m (horizontal)
    - At impact: velocity vector at 45° below horizontal

Free Response Questions (FRQ) 1–10

FRQ 1

Experimental Design: Measuring g

A student wants to measure g using a ball drop and stopwatch.

(a) Describe the experimental setup. What measurements are taken? (b) Write the equation relating h, g, and t for a ball dropped from rest. (c) The student measures h=2.00 m and t=0.638 s. Calculate g. (d) Identify two sources of error and their effect on the measured g. (e) How could the student improve accuracy?

Show worked answer

Answer Key:

(a) Drop ball from measured height h, measure time t to reach ground.
    Measurements: height with meter stick, time with stopwatch (or photogate).

(b) h = ½gt²  →  g = 2h/t²

(c) g = 2(2.00)/(0.638)² = 4.00/0.407 = 9.83 m/s²

(d) Sources:
    - Human reaction time: makes t larger → calculated g smaller than actual
    - Air resistance: makes t larger → calculated g smaller than actual

(e) Use photogate timers for precise measurement; average many trials;
    use longer drop heights to reduce reaction time error percentage.
FRQ 2

Kinematics Graph Analysis

A particle moves along the x-axis. Its x-t graph shows:

  • Segment 1 (0→2 s): starts at x=0, curves up to x=8 m
  • Segment 2 (2→5 s): straight line from x=8 to x=−4 m
  • Segment 3 (5→7 s): horizontal line at x=−4 m

(a) During which segment is acceleration nonzero? (b) Find average velocity during Segment 2. (c) At what time is the object nearest to origin after t=2 s? (d) Sketch the corresponding v-t graph.

Show worked answer

Answer Key:

(a) Segment 1 (curved x-t → changing slope → nonzero acceleration)

(b) v_avg = Δx/Δt = (−4 − 8)/(5 − 2) = −12/3 = −4 m/s

(c) During Segment 2: x crosses zero when
    x(t) = 8 + (−4)(t − 2) = 8 − 4t + 8 = 16 − 4t = 0
    t = 4 s
    At t=5 s: x=−4 m, so nearest to origin at t=4 s (x=0)

(d) v-t sketch:
    Segment 1: positive, increasing from 0 (positive acceleration)
    Segment 2: constant −4 m/s (straight horizontal line at v=−4)
    Segment 3: v = 0 (horizontal line at v=0)
FRQ 3

Projectile Motion: Complete Analysis

A ball is kicked from ground level at v₀=18 m/s at 53° above horizontal (sin53°=0.80, cos53°=0.60, g=10 m/s²).

(a) Find initial velocity components. (b) Find maximum height. (c) Find total time of flight. (d) Find horizontal range. (e) Find velocity (magnitude and direction) at t=1.0 s. (f) At what two times is the ball at height 5 m?

Show worked answer

Answer Key:

(a) v₀ₓ = 18(0.60) = 10.8 m/s
    v₀ᵧ = 18(0.80) = 14.4 m/s

(b) H = v₀ᵧ²/2g = (14.4)²/20 = 207.36/20 = 10.37 m

(c) T = 2v₀ᵧ/g = 2(14.4)/10 = 2.88 s

(d) R = v₀ₓ × T = 10.8 × 2.88 = 31.1 m

(e) At t=1.0 s:
    vₓ = 10.8 m/s (constant)
    vᵧ = 14.4 − 10(1.0) = 4.4 m/s (upward)
    |v| = √(10.8² + 4.4²) = √(116.6 + 19.4) = √136 = 11.7 m/s
    θ = arctan(4.4/10.8) = 22.2° above horizontal

(f) 5 = 14.4t − 5t²
    5t² − 14.4t + 5 = 0
    t = [14.4 ± √(207.4 − 100)]/10 = [14.4 ± √107.4]/10
    t = [14.4 ± 10.36]/10
    t₁ = 0.404 s (going up)
    t₂ = 2.48 s (coming down)
FRQ 4

Relative Motion

A passenger walks forward at 1.5 m/s relative to a train car. The train moves east at 25 m/s relative to the ground. A bird flies west at 10 m/s relative to ground.

(a) Find passenger's velocity relative to ground. (b) Find passenger's velocity relative to the bird. (c) Find the train's velocity relative to the bird. (d) How long does it take the bird to fly 500 m relative to the ground?

Show worked answer

Answer Key:

(a) v_passenger/ground = v_passenger/train + v_train/ground
    = +1.5 + 25 = 26.5 m/s east

(b) v_passenger/bird = v_passenger/ground − v_bird/ground
    = 26.5 − (−10) = 36.5 m/s east

(c) v_train/bird = 25 − (−10) = 35 m/s east

(d) t = 500/10 = 50 s
FRQ 5

Multi-Object Problem

Object A: starts at x=0 with v=8 m/s, a=0. Object B: starts at x=−30 m with v=0, a=3 m/s².

(a) Write position equations for A and B. (b) Find when they are at the same position. (c) Find their velocities at that time. (d) Sketch x-t graph for both from t=0 to t=6 s.

Show worked answer

Answer Key:

(a) x_A = 8t
    x_B = −30 + ½(3)t² = −30 + 1.5t²

(b) Set equal: 8t = −30 + 1.5t²
    1.5t² − 8t − 30 = 0
    t = [8 ± √(64 + 180)]/3 = [8 ± √244]/3
    t = [8 ± 15.62]/3
    Take positive: t = (8 + 15.62)/3 = 7.87 s

(c) v_A = 8 m/s (constant)
    v_B = 3(7.87) = 23.6 m/s

(d) x_A: straight line from (0,0) to (6,48)
    x_B: parabola starting at (0,−30) curving upward
    They haven't met yet at t=6 s (meet at t=7.87 s)
FRQ 6

Cliff Projectile Analysis

A cliff is 60 m high. A ball is launched horizontally from the top.

(a) Derive an expression for time to hit ground. (b) Derive an expression for horizontal range in terms of v₀ and H. (c) If v₀=15 m/s, find range and impact speed. (g=9.8 m/s²) (d) What angle does velocity make with horizontal at impact?

Show worked answer

Answer Key:

(a) H = ½gt²  →  t = √(2H/g)

(b) R = v₀t = v₀√(2H/g)

(c) t = √(2×60/9.8) = √12.24 = 3.50 s
    R = 15 × 3.50 = 52.5 m
    
    vₓ = 15 m/s
    vᵧ = 9.8(3.50) = 34.3 m/s
    v = √(15² + 34.3²) = √(225 + 1176) = √1401 = 37.4 m/s

(d) θ = arctan(34.3/15) = arctan(2.29) = 66.4° below horizontal
FRQ 7

Non-Constant Acceleration

A particle's velocity is v(t) = 6t² − 4t + 2 m/s. At t=0, x=5 m.

(a) Find acceleration at t=3 s. (b) Find position at t=2 s. (c) Find when acceleration equals zero. (d) Explain the physical significance of a=0 in terms of the v-t graph.

Show worked answer

Answer Key:

(a) a(t) = dv/dt = 12t − 4
    a(3) = 12(3) − 4 = 36 − 4 = 32 m/s²

(b) x(t) = x₀ + ∫₀ᵗ v dt = 5 + ∫₀² (6t² − 4t + 2) dt
    = 5 + [2t³ − 2t² + 2t]₀²
    = 5 + [16 − 8 + 4 − 0]
    = 5 + 12 = 17 m

(c) 12t − 4 = 0  →  t = 1/3 s

(d) a=0 means the v-t graph has zero slope at that instant —
    it's a local minimum or maximum of velocity.
    At t=1/3 s, velocity = 6(1/9) − 4(1/3) + 2 = 2/3 − 4/3 + 2 = 4/3 m/s
    This is the minimum velocity of the particle.
FRQ 8

Experimental: Measuring Projectile Range

A student launches steel balls horizontally from a ramp at varying heights h above the launch point. The ball lands at horizontal distance d from the base of a table of height H.

(a) What two measurements must be made for each trial? (b) Explain which variable determines time of flight. (c) Derive d as a function of v₀ and H. (d) If H=0.80 m and the student measures d=1.20 m, find v₀. (e) The student graphs d vs v₀. What shape is expected and why?

Show worked answer

Answer Key:

(a) Horizontal distance d from base of table, and launch speed v₀
    (measured using other kinematics or energy method)

(b) Table height H determines time of flight: t = √(2H/g)
    (independent of v₀ — vertical and horizontal motions independent)

(c) t = √(2H/g)
    d = v₀t = v₀√(2H/g)

(d) v₀ = d/√(2H/g) = 1.20/√(1.60/9.8) = 1.20/√0.163 = 1.20/0.404 = 2.97 m/s

(e) d = v₀ × constant, so d vs v₀ is a straight line through origin.
    Slope = √(2H/g) = constant depending on table height.
FRQ 9

Multi-part: Vertical Throw Analysis

A ball is thrown upward at v₀=15 m/s from a building roof 30 m high. (g=9.8 m/s²)

(a) Find max height above ground. (b) Find time to reach max height. (c) Find total time to hit ground. (d) Find speed when it passes the rooftop level on the way down. (e) Find speed at ground impact.

Show worked answer

Answer Key:

(a) H_max = 30 + v₀²/2g = 30 + (225/19.6) = 30 + 11.48 = 41.5 m

(b) t_peak = v₀/g = 15/9.8 = 1.53 s

(c) Total fall from peak to ground:
    h_total = 41.5 m from ground
    h = ½gt² → t_fall = √(2×41.5/9.8) = √8.47 = 2.91 s
    Total time = t_up + t_fall = 1.53 + 2.91 = 4.44 s
    
    OR: −30 = 15t − 4.9t²
    4.9t² − 15t − 30 = 0
    t = [15 ± √(225 + 588)]/9.8 = [15 ± 28.5]/9.8
    t = 43.5/9.8 = 4.44 s ✓

(d) At roof level (y = 30 m, same height as launch):
    v² = v₀² = 225 → v = 15 m/s (downward by symmetry)

(e) v = √(v₀² + 2g×30) = √(225 + 588) = √813 = 28.5 m/s
FRQ 10

Synthesis: Chase Problem

A police car at rest begins pursuit when a speeder passes at 30 m/s. The police car accelerates at 4 m/s².

(a) Write equations for position of each vehicle. (b) How long until police car catches the speeder? (c) How far from the starting point? (d) What is the police car's speed when it catches the speeder? (e) At what time does the police car match the speeder's speed?

Show worked answer

Answer Key:

(a) x_speeder = 30t
    x_police = ½(4)t² = 2t²

(b) Set equal: 2t² = 30t
    2t² − 30t = 0
    2t(t − 15) = 0
    t = 0 (start) or t = 15 s

(c) x = 30(15) = 450 m

(d) v_police = at = 4(15) = 60 m/s

(e) Police matches speeder's speed when v_police = 30 m/s
    4t = 30  →  t = 7.5 s
    (At this point police is still behind; hasn't caught up yet)
    Position check: x_police(7.5) = 2(56.25) = 112.5 m
                    x_speeder(7.5) = 30(7.5) = 225 m → 112.5 m behind

Force & Dynamics

Newton's Laws · Friction · Free Body Diagrams

AP Physics 1 | Georgia Standards of Excellence College Board CED Topic: DYN-1 through DYN-5

2.1

The Concept of Force and Newton's First Law

Force is the fundamental agent of change in mechanics. Formally, a force is any interaction between two objects that can cause acceleration — a push or pull that tends to change an object's state of motion. Forces are vectors: they have both magnitude (measured in Newtons, where 1 N = 1 kg·m/s²) and direction. Multiple forces acting on the same object combine by vector addition to produce a single net force, ΣF.

Newton's First Law (Law of Inertia): An object at rest remains at rest, and an object moving with constant velocity continues at that constant velocity, unless acted upon by a nonzero net external force. This law defines a class of reference frames called inertial frames — frames that are not themselves accelerating — within which all of Newton's laws hold exactly.

Inertia is the intrinsic resistance of matter to changes in its state of motion. It is measured by mass: a more massive object requires a larger force to achieve the same acceleration. This is not a separate law — it is the physical content encoded in F = ma when ΣF = 0 gives a = 0.

Equilibrium is the condition ΣF = 0. An object in equilibrium either remains stationary (static equilibrium) or moves at constant velocity (dynamic equilibrium). The critical point: equilibrium does not mean "nothing is happening" — it means the forces are balanced. A car cruising at constant highway speed is in dynamic equilibrium despite the engine producing thrust, because drag exactly equals the driving force.

ΣF = 0  ⟹  a = 0  (at rest OR constant velocity)
ΣF ≠ 0  ⟹  a ≠ 0  (acceleration — speed or direction changes)

Newton's 1st Law is the special case of 2nd Law when a = 0.
2.2

Newton's Second Law

Newton's Second Law is the central equation of classical mechanics: ΣF = ma. The net force on an object equals the product of its mass and acceleration. It is a vector equation — it applies separately and independently in each direction. You will almost always decompose it into x and y components when solving problems: ΣFₓ = maₓ and ΣFᵧ = maᵧ.

The law tells us that force causes acceleration — not velocity. A constant net force does not produce a constant velocity; it produces a constant acceleration, which means ever-increasing velocity. This is why a rocket under constant thrust continues to speed up rather than maintaining a fixed velocity.

Weight and mass are different quantities that students frequently confuse. Mass (m) is an intrinsic property of matter — a measure of inertia — that does not change with location. Weight (W) is the gravitational force on an object: W = mg, where g is the local gravitational field strength (9.8 m/s² near Earth's surface, ~1.6 m/s² on the Moon). On the Moon, your mass is identical to what it is on Earth, but your weight is about 1/6 as large.

Systematic method for applying Newton's Second Law: (1) Identify the system (which object?). (2) Draw a free-body diagram showing all forces on that object. (3) Choose a coordinate system. (4) Write ΣFₓ = maₓ and ΣFᵧ = maᵧ. (5) Solve algebraically. This procedure works for every problem, no matter how complicated.

ΣF = ma    (vector: applies in ALL directions simultaneously)
ΣFₓ = maₓ  ΣFᵧ = maᵧ   (component equations)

Weight:  W = mg    [N]    g = 9.8 m/s² (Earth surface)
Mass:    m = W/g   [kg]   — invariant, does not change with location

Corollaries:
  a = ΣF/m  → greater mass = smaller acceleration for same force
  m = ΣF/a  → mass can be measured from force and acceleration
2.3

Newton's Third Law: Action-Reaction Pairs

Newton's Third Law states that whenever object A exerts a force on object B, object B simultaneously exerts an equal-magnitude, opposite-direction force on object A. These two forces — an action-reaction pair — always occur together and are simultaneous; one cannot exist without the other.

The single most important rule: Third Law force pairs always act on different objects. This means they never cancel each other in the analysis of any single object's motion. Many students mistakenly argue: "If every force has an equal and opposite reaction, how can anything ever accelerate?" The error is thinking the paired forces act on the same object. The net force on a single object includes only the forces acting ON that object, and those do not cancel unless the object happens to be in equilibrium.

Identifying Third Law pairs correctly: The forces must be (a) equal in magnitude, (b) opposite in direction, (c) the same type of force, and (d) acting on different objects. A common misconception on AP exams: students identify weight and normal force as a Third Law pair. They are not — both act on the same object (the book). They cancel because the book is in equilibrium, which is a consequence of Newton's Second Law (ΣF = 0), not Newton's Third Law.

Newton's 3rd Law: F_AB = −F_BA (equal magnitude, opposite direction)

Example — Book at rest on table:
  Pair 1: Earth pulls book DOWN (gravity)
          Book pulls Earth UP (gravity) ← 3rd Law pair ✓
  Pair 2: Table pushes book UP (normal)
          Book pushes table DOWN (normal) ← 3rd Law pair ✓

MISCONCEPTION: Weight and Normal are NOT a 3rd Law pair
  (Both act on the book; they cancel because ΣF=0, not because of 3rd Law)
2.4

Catalog of Common Forces

In AP Physics problems, most scenarios involve a small set of named forces. Understanding the nature and direction of each is essential before drawing a correct free-body diagram.

Normal Force (N): A contact force perpendicular to the surface between two objects, arising from the electromagnetic repulsion between surface atoms. It adjusts dynamically to whatever value prevents penetration of one surface by another. On a flat horizontal surface with no other vertical forces, N = mg. On an incline at angle θ, the component of gravity perpendicular to the surface is mg cosθ, so N = mg cosθ. If you push an object into a surface with extra force, N increases; if you pull an object away from the surface, N decreases — and if pulled hard enough, the surface loses contact and N = 0.

Friction (f): A contact force parallel to the surface opposing relative motion or the tendency of relative motion. Static friction (fₛ) prevents an object from starting to slide; it ranges from zero up to a maximum fₛ,max = μₛN. Kinetic friction (fₖ) acts on sliding objects with a fixed magnitude fₖ = μₖN, always directed opposite to the velocity of sliding. Since μₛ > μₖ always, it takes more force to start an object moving than to keep it moving — a familiar everyday experience.

Tension (T): The pulling force transmitted through a flexible connector (rope, string, cable, chain). It always acts along the connector and away from the object. For a massless, inextensible rope, the tension is identical at every point along it. In AP problems, ropes and strings are treated as ideal (massless) unless stated otherwise.

Spring Force — Hooke's Law: A spring exerts a restoring force F = −kx, where x is the displacement from the spring's natural (equilibrium) length and k is the spring constant in N/m. The negative sign reflects that the spring always pushes back toward equilibrium, opposing the displacement.

NORMAL FORCE:
  Flat horizontal surface:      N = mg
  Inclined plane (angle θ):     N = mg cosθ
  Extra downward push (angle φ): N = mg + F sinφ
  Extra upward pull (angle φ):  N = mg − F sinφ

FRICTION:
  Static:  fₛ ≤ μₛN  (max when object on verge of sliding)
  Kinetic: fₖ = μₖN  (constant; direction opposes sliding velocity)
  Always:  μₛ > μₖ

SPRING (Hooke's Law):
  F_spring = −kx    k in N/m, x = stretch/compression in m
2.5

Dynamics on Inclines and the Atwood Machine

Inclined plane: The standard technique is to tilt the coordinate system so x runs along the slope (down the incline as positive) and y runs perpendicular to it. In this tilted frame, the component of weight parallel to the slope is mg sinθ (pointing down the incline) and the component perpendicular is mg cosθ (into the surface). The normal force equals mg cosθ. If the block slides down with kinetic friction μₖ acting up the slope, Newton's Second Law along the incline gives: mg sinθ − μₖmg cosθ = ma, so a = g(sinθ − μₖ cosθ).

Atwood machine: Two masses m₁ and m₂ (m₁ > m₂) are connected by a massless string over a frictionless, massless pulley. The system is treated as a whole: the net force causing acceleration is (m₁ − m₂)g (the weight difference), and the total mass being accelerated is (m₁ + m₂). Dividing gives the magnitude of acceleration. To find the tension, apply Newton's Second Law to either mass individually, using the acceleration already found.

INCLINED PLANE (sliding down, kinetic friction):
  N = mg cosθ                        (perpendicular — equilibrium)
  mg sinθ − μₖmg cosθ = ma          (along slope — net force)
  a = g(sinθ − μₖ cosθ)

ATWOOD MACHINE (m₁ > m₂, ideal pulley + string):
  Net force on system: (m₁ − m₂)g = (m₁ + m₂)a
  a = (m₁ − m₂)g / (m₁ + m₂)
  Tension: T = m₂(g + a) = 2m₁m₂g / (m₁ + m₂)
2.1

Free Body Diagram: All Forces on One Object

A free body diagram isolates ONE object and shows ALL forces acting ON it — never forces it exerts on others. Arrows start at the object and point in the force direction. Choose a coordinate system aligned with acceleration for the simplest equations.

Text version of this diagram
Block sliding right on rough surface:

          ↑ N (Normal — perpendicular to surface, from surface)
          │
 F_app → [m] ← fk (kinetic friction — opposes sliding, points LEFT)
          │
          ↓ mg (Weight — always straight down)

ΣFx = F_app − fk = ma     (x-direction, with friction)
ΣFy = N − mg = 0          (y-direction, no vertical acceleration)

fk = μk N = μk mg         (substitute to find a)
2.2

Inclined Plane: Tilted Coordinate System

Tilt axes to align with the slope. Weight always points straight down but splits into components parallel (mg sinθ, causes sliding) and perpendicular (mg cosθ, balanced by N) to the slope surface.

Text version of this diagram
         ↑ N (perpendicular to slope)
        /
       / object [m]
      /────────── x' (along slope, down = positive)
     /  mg cosθ ↙   mg sinθ → (along slope, causes acceleration)
    /
  θ/___________________________

N = mg cosθ                      (perpendicular equilibrium)
ma = mg sinθ − μk mg cosθ        (along slope: gravity − friction)
a = g(sinθ − μk cosθ)            (if sliding down with friction)
2.3

Newton's Third Law: Action-Reaction Pairs

Third Law pairs always act on DIFFERENT objects. They are always the same type, equal magnitude, opposite direction — but never cancel in any single object's Newton's Second Law analysis.

Text version of this diagram
Book at rest on table:

Earth pulls book DOWN (gravity, on book)        ─┐
Book pulls Earth UP (gravity, on Earth)         ─┘ 3rd Law pair

Table pushes book UP (normal, on book)          ─┐
Book pushes table DOWN (normal, on table)       ─┘ 3rd Law pair

For the BOOK alone (FBD):
  ↑ N (from table, on book)
  [book]
  ↓ mg (from Earth, on book)

  ΣF = N − mg = 0  (book at rest)
  This is 2nd Law (equilibrium) — NOT 3rd Law cancellation!
Example 2.1

Finding Net Force

Algebraic Calculation

Question: Three forces act on a 5 kg box: 30 N east, 10 N west, 20 N north. Find (a) net force, (b) acceleration magnitude.

Show solution

Solution:

(a) ΣFₓ = 30 − 10 = 20 N east
    ΣFᵧ = 20 N north
    ΣF = √(20² + 20²) = √800 = 28.3 N at 45° north of east

(b) a = ΣF/m = 28.3/5 = 5.66 m/s²
Example 2.2

Normal Force on Flat Surface

Algebraic Calculation

Question: A 60 kg person stands in an elevator. Find normal force when elevator (a) at rest, (b) accelerating up at 2 m/s², (c) accelerating down at 3 m/s².

Show solution

Solution:

(a) ΣFᵧ = 0: N − mg = 0 → N = mg = 60(9.8) = 588 N

(b) ΣFᵧ = maᵧ (up positive): N − mg = ma
    N = m(g + a) = 60(9.8 + 2) = 60(11.8) = 708 N

(c) N − mg = m(−a): N = m(g − a) = 60(9.8 − 3) = 60(6.8) = 408 N

Note: Feel heavier when accelerating up; lighter when accelerating down
Example 2.3

Friction on Flat Surface

Algebraic Calculation

Question: A 10 kg box (μₛ=0.50, μₖ=0.35) is pushed with 40 N. Does it move? If so, find acceleration.

Show solution

Solution:

Normal force: N = mg = 10(9.8) = 98 N
Max static friction: fₛ_max = μₛN = 0.50(98) = 49 N

Applied force = 40 N < fₛ_max = 49 N
→ Box does NOT move (static friction = 40 N, no acceleration)

If pushed with 60 N (> 49 N):
Box moves. Kinetic friction: fₖ = μₖN = 0.35(98) = 34.3 N
ΣF = 60 − 34.3 = 25.7 N
a = F/m = 25.7/10 = 2.57 m/s²
Example 2.4

Inclined Plane: No Friction

Algebraic Calculation

Question: A 5 kg block slides down a frictionless 30° incline. Find acceleration and normal force.

Show solution

Solution:

Coordinate system: x = down incline (+), y = ⊥ to incline (+away from surface)

ΣFᵧ = 0: N − mg cos30° = 0
  N = 5(9.8)(cos30°) = 49(0.866) = 42.4 N

ΣFₓ = maₓ: mg sin30° = ma
  a = g sin30° = 9.8(0.5) = 4.9 m/s² (down the incline)
Example 2.5

Inclined Plane with Friction

Algebraic Calculation

Question: An 8 kg block on a 37° incline has μₖ = 0.

  1. (sin37°=0.6, cos37°=0.8) Find acceleration when sliding down.
Show solution

Solution:

N = mg cos37° = 8(9.8)(0.8) = 62.7 N
fₖ = μₖN = 0.25(62.7) = 15.7 N (up the incline, opposing motion)
W∥ = mg sin37° = 8(9.8)(0.6) = 47.0 N (down the incline)

ΣFₓ: mg sin37° − fₖ = ma
47.0 − 15.7 = 8a
31.3 = 8a
a = 3.91 m/s² (down the incline)
Example 2.6

Atwood Machine

Algebraic Calculation

Question: Two masses m₁=8 kg and m₂=3 kg hang over a frictionless pulley. Find acceleration and tension.

Show solution

Solution:

a = (m₁ − m₂)g/(m₁ + m₂) = (8−3)(9.8)/(8+3) = 5(9.8)/11 = 4.45 m/s²

T = 2m₁m₂g/(m₁+m₂) = 2(8)(3)(9.8)/11 = 470.4/11 = 42.8 N

Verify with individual equations:
  m₁: m₁g − T = m₁a → 78.4 − T = 8(4.45) = 35.6 → T = 42.8 N ✓
  m₂: T − m₂g = m₂a → T − 29.4 = 3(4.45) = 13.4 → T = 42.8 N ✓
Example 2.7

Connected Objects (Horizontal)

Algebraic Calculation

Question: A 3 kg box (A) is connected by string to a 5 kg box (B) on a frictionless surface. Force F=24 N pulls B. Find (a) acceleration of system, (b) tension in string.

Show solution

Solution:

(a) Treat as system: ΣF = (m_A + m_B)a
    24 = (3 + 5)a = 8a
    a = 3 m/s²

(b) Tension acts only on box A:
    T = m_A × a = 3 × 3 = 9 N

    Verify for B: F − T = m_B × a
    24 − 9 = 5(3) = 15 ✓
Example 2.8

Static Equilibrium

Algebraic Calculation

Question: A 5 kg sign is suspended from two wires making 30° and 60° with horizontal. Find tension in each wire.

Show solution

Solution:

Weight: W = 5(9.8) = 49 N

Equilibrium conditions:
ΣFₓ = 0: T₂cos60° − T₁cos30° = 0     → T₂(0.5) = T₁(0.866)
ΣFᵧ = 0: T₁sin30° + T₂sin60° = W     → 0.5T₁ + 0.866T₂ = 49

From first equation: T₂ = 1.732T₁
Substitute: 0.5T₁ + 0.866(1.732T₁) = 49
            0.5T₁ + 1.5T₁ = 49
            2T₁ = 49
            T₁ = 24.5 N
            T₂ = 1.732(24.5) = 42.4 N
Example 2.9

Third Law Application

Qualitative Reasoning

Question: A horse pulls a cart with force F. The cart pulls back on the horse with equal force F (Newton's 3rd Law). So why does the cart accelerate?

Show solution

Solution:

The 3rd law pair forces DO cancel in total — but they act on DIFFERENT objects:

  • Force from horse on cart → accelerates the CART
  • Force from cart on horse → this is just ONE force on the horse


The horse also has external friction from the ground (forward push).
Net force on horse = ground friction − cart's pull on horse ≠ 0

Net force on CART = horse's pull on cart − any friction on cart ≠ 0

Key insight: Newton's 3rd law pairs cannot cancel each other
because they act on different objects. Each object has its own FBD.
Example 2.10

Finding Coefficient of Friction

Algebraic Calculation

Question: A 20 kg block slides across a floor and decelerates from 8 m/s to rest in 4 m. Find (a) deceleration, (b) friction force, (c) coefficient of kinetic friction.

Show solution

Solution:

(a) v² = v₀² + 2aΔx
    0 = 64 + 2a(4)
    a = −8 m/s² (deceleration of 8 m/s²)

(b) fₖ = ma = 20(8) = 160 N

(c) N = mg = 20(9.8) = 196 N
    μₖ = fₖ/N = 160/196 = 0.816
Example 2.11

Tension in Hanging System

Algebraic Calculation

Question: Three blocks hang vertically: A (2 kg) below B (3 kg) below C (4 kg) from a ceiling. Find tension in each rope segment.

Show solution

Solution:

Rope below C holds A and B:
  T₁ = (m_A + m_B)g = (2+3)(9.8) = 49 N

Rope below ceiling holds all three... wait, re-read:
  C hangs from ceiling, B hangs from C, A hangs from B

Rope 1 (A to B): T₁ = m_A × g = 2(9.8) = 19.6 N
Rope 2 (B to C): T₂ = (m_A + m_B)g = 5(9.8) = 49 N
Rope 3 (C to ceiling): T₃ = (m_A + m_B + m_C)g = 9(9.8) = 88.2 N
Example 2.12

Apparent Weight in Circular Motion

Algebraic Calculation

Question: A 70 kg person rides at top and bottom of a Ferris wheel (radius 10 m, speed 6 m/s). Find apparent weight at each position. (g=9.8 m/s²)

Show solution

Solution:

Centripetal acceleration: aₒ = v²/r = 36/10 = 3.6 m/s²

At TOP (centripetal direction = downward):
  mg − N = maₒ
  N = m(g − aₒ) = 70(9.8 − 3.6) = 70(6.2) = 434 N

At BOTTOM (centripetal direction = upward):
  N − mg = maₒ
  N = m(g + aₒ) = 70(9.8 + 3.6) = 70(13.4) = 938 N
Example 2.13

Pulley with Friction

Algebraic Calculation

Question: Mass A (4 kg) sits on surface (μₖ=0.30) and is connected by rope over pulley to hanging mass B (3 kg). Find acceleration.

Show solution

Solution:

N_A = m_A × g = 4(9.8) = 39.2 N
fₖ = μₖN_A = 0.30(39.2) = 11.76 N

For system (B falls, A slides):
  Net force = m_B × g − fₖ = 3(9.8) − 11.76 = 29.4 − 11.76 = 17.64 N
  Total mass = m_A + m_B = 7 kg
  a = 17.64/7 = 2.52 m/s²

Check with individual equations:
  B: m_B g − T = m_B a → 29.4 − T = 3(2.52) = 7.56 → T = 21.84 N
  A: T − fₖ = m_A a → 21.84 − 11.76 = 10.08 = 4(2.52) ✓
Example 2.14

Force at Angle

Algebraic Calculation

Question: A 15 kg crate is pulled at 30° above horizontal with 80 N. μₖ=0.

  1. Find acceleration.
Show solution

Solution:

Horizontal: Fₓ = 80 cos30° = 80(0.866) = 69.3 N
Vertical: Fᵧ = 80 sin30° = 80(0.5) = 40 N (upward)

Normal force (vertical equilibrium):
N + Fᵧ − mg = 0
N = mg − Fᵧ = 15(9.8) − 40 = 147 − 40 = 107 N

Kinetic friction: fₖ = μₖN = 0.20(107) = 21.4 N

Newton's 2nd (horizontal): Fₓ − fₖ = ma
69.3 − 21.4 = 15a
47.9 = 15a
a = 3.19 m/s²
Example 2.15

Minimum Force to Prevent Sliding

Algebraic Calculation

Question: A 2 kg block sits on a 40° incline. What minimum force parallel to incline (up) prevents sliding? (μₛ=0.35)

Show solution

Solution:

N = mg cos40° = 2(9.8)(0.766) = 15.0 N
Max static friction: fₛ = μₛN = 0.35(15.0) = 5.25 N (up the incline)
Weight component: W∥ = mg sin40° = 2(9.8)(0.643) = 12.6 N (down)

At minimum force F (up incline) to prevent sliding down:
F + fₛ = W∥ (friction also acts up when trying to prevent sliding down)
F = W∥ − fₛ = 12.6 − 5.25 = 7.35 N
Example 2.16

Newton's 3rd Law: Recoil

Qualitative Reasoning + Calculation

Question: A 75 kg person on ice skates pushes off a 100 kg wall. The wall pushes them back with 300 N for 0.5 s. Find (a) acceleration of person, (b) final velocity of person.

Show solution

Solution:

(a) By Newton's 3rd Law, person experiences 300 N force.
    a = F/m = 300/75 = 4 m/s²

(b) v = v₀ + at = 0 + 4(0.5) = 2 m/s (away from wall)

Note: Wall doesn't move (attached to Earth, effectively infinite mass)
      If wall were a free-standing block of 100 kg:
      a_wall = 300/100 = 3 m/s² (equal and opposite force)
Example 2.17

Spring Force and Equilibrium

Algebraic Calculation

Question: A spring (k=200 N/m) is attached to ceiling. A 500 g mass hangs from it. (a) How far does spring stretch? (b) What additional mass makes it stretch 8 cm total?

Show solution

Solution:

(a) At equilibrium: F_spring = weight
    kx = mg
    200x = 0.5(9.8) = 4.9 N
    x = 4.9/200 = 0.0245 m = 2.45 cm

(b) For total stretch x = 0.08 m:
    kx = Mg
    200(0.08) = Mg
    16 = Mg
    M = 16/9.8 = 1.633 kg
    Additional mass = 1.633 − 0.5 = 1.133 kg
Example 2.18

Two-Block Push

Algebraic Calculation

Question: Force F=30 N pushes two blocks (m₁=4 kg, m₂=6 kg) on frictionless floor. Find (a) acceleration, (b) contact force between blocks.

Show solution

Solution:

(a) F = (m₁ + m₂)a
    30 = (4+6)a = 10a
    a = 3 m/s²

(b) Contact force on m₂ from m₁:
    F_contact = m₂ × a = 6 × 3 = 18 N

    Check on m₁: F − F_contact = m₁ × a
    30 − 18 = 12 = 4(3) ✓
Example 2.19

Calculus: Variable Force

Calculus Derivation (AP-C Level)

Question: A force F(t) = (6t − 4) N acts on a 2 kg object. At t=0, v=3 m/s. Find v(t) and v at t=3 s.

Show solution

Solution:

F = ma → a(t) = F(t)/m = (6t−4)/2 = 3t − 2

v(t) = v₀ + ∫₀ᵗ a dt = 3 + ∫₀ᵗ (3t−2) dt
     = 3 + [3t²/2 − 2t]₀ᵗ
     = 3 + 3t²/2 − 2t
     = 3t²/2 − 2t + 3

v(3) = 3(9)/2 − 2(3) + 3 = 13.5 − 6 + 3 = 10.5 m/s
Example 2.20

AP FRQ: Inclined Plane System

Free Response Question

Question: Block A (m_A=3 kg) sits on a 30° frictionless incline. It is connected by massless string over a frictionless pulley to hanging Block B (m_B=2 kg).

(a) Draw FBDs for each block. (b) Determine which block accelerates down/up. (c) Find acceleration of system. (d) Find tension in string. (e) If μₖ=0.20 is added to incline, find new acceleration.

Show solution

Solution:

(a) FBD Block A (on incline):
    - Weight mg_A down
    - Normal N perpendicular to incline  
    - Tension T up the incline
    
    FBD Block B (hanging):
    - Weight mg_B down
    - Tension T upward

(b) Compare forces:
    Tendency of A to slide down: m_A g sin30° = 3(9.8)(0.5) = 14.7 N
    Weight of B: m_B g = 2(9.8) = 19.6 N
    B is heavier → B descends, A moves UP the incline

(c) For B (down): m_B g − T = m_B a
    For A (up incline): T − m_A g sin30° = m_A a
    
    Add: m_B g − m_A g sin30° = (m_A + m_B)a
    19.6 − 14.7 = 5a
    4.9 = 5a
    a = 0.98 m/s²

(d) T = m_A(a + g sin30°) = 3(0.98 + 4.9) = 3(5.88) = 17.6 N
    Check: T = m_B(g − a) = 2(9.8 − 0.98) = 2(8.82) = 17.6 N ✓

(e) With friction (A now moving UP, friction acts DOWN incline):
    N = m_A g cos30° = 3(9.8)(0.866) = 25.5 N
    fₖ = μₖN = 0.20(25.5) = 5.10 N (DOWN incline, opposing upward motion)
    
    m_B g − T = m_B a
    T − m_A g sin30° − fₖ = m_A a
    
    Add: m_B g − m_A g sin30° − fₖ = (m_A + m_B)a
    19.6 − 14.7 − 5.10 = 5a
    −0.2 = 5a
    a = −0.04 m/s² 
    
    Negative means our assumed direction was wrong — 
    actually A slides DOWN and B goes UP, OR system is in static equilibrium.
    Check static: net tendency = −0.2 N → static friction can hold this → EQUILIBRIUM

Free Response Questions (FRQ) 1–10

FRQ 1

Experimental Design: Measuring Friction

A student places a block on an inclined board and measures the angle at which it just starts to slide.

(a) What angle measurement gives μₛ? Derive the relationship. (b) If critical angle = 32°, calculate μₛ. (c) The student tilts faster and measures sliding angle = 28°. Calculate μₖ. (d) Explain why μₛ > μₖ conceptually.

Show worked answer

Answer:

(a) At critical angle: mg sinθ = μₛ mg cosθ → μₛ = tanθ
(b) μₛ = tan32° = 0.625
(c) μₖ = tan28° = 0.532
(d) Static friction must be broken (molecular bonds stronger when stationary);
    kinetic friction: sliding surfaces have less contact time → lower coefficient
FRQ 2

Inclined Plane with Connected Mass

Block A (5 kg) on 37° incline (μₖ=0.20) connects via string over pulley to hanging Block B.

(a) Find minimum mass of B to start A moving UP the incline. (b) If m_B = 4 kg, find acceleration direction and magnitude. (c) Find tension in string for part (b).

Show worked answer

Answer:

(a) For A to just start moving up:
    T = m_A g sin37° + μₛ m_A g cos37°
    For minimum: T = m_B g
    m_B g = 5(9.8)(0.6) + 0.20(5)(9.8)(0.8) = 29.4 + 7.84 = 37.24 N
    m_B = 3.80 kg

(b) With m_B=4: 
    Tendency force of B down = 4(9.8)=39.2 N
    Resistance of A = 29.4+7.84=37.24 N (sin+kinetic friction)
    Net = 39.2−37.24 = 1.96 N → A moves UP
    a = 1.96/(5+4) = 0.218 m/s²

(c) T = m_B(g−a) = 4(9.8−0.218) = 38.3 N
FRQ 3

Newton's Laws: Acceleration Analysis

A 10 kg sled is pulled by rope at 25° above horizontal with force 60 N on a surface with μₖ=0.15.

(a) Draw complete FBD. (b) Calculate normal force. (c) Calculate kinetic friction. (d) Calculate acceleration. (e) If rope is cut, calculate deceleration due to friction.

Show worked answer

Answer:

(a) FBD: Weight mg down, Normal N up, Applied F at 25° above horizontal, Friction fₖ backward

(b) N = mg − F sin25° = 10(9.8) − 60(0.423) = 98 − 25.4 = 72.6 N

(c) fₖ = μₖN = 0.15(72.6) = 10.9 N

(d) ΣFₓ = F cos25° − fₖ = 60(0.906) − 10.9 = 54.4 − 10.9 = 43.5 N
    a = 43.5/10 = 4.35 m/s²

(e) After rope cut: fₖ = μₖmg = 0.15(10)(9.8) = 14.7 N (larger, full weight now)
    a = −fₖ/m = −14.7/10 = −1.47 m/s²
FRQ 4

Elevator Problem

A person (mass 65 kg) stands on a scale in an elevator.

(a) Scale reading at rest. (b) Scale reading: accelerating up at 1.5 m/s². (c) Scale reading: accelerating down at 2.0 m/s². (d) Velocity at which person feels 80% of normal weight. (e) At what acceleration does the person feel "weightless"?

Show worked answer

Answer:

(a) N = mg = 65(9.8) = 637 N
(b) N = m(g+a) = 65(11.3) = 734.5 N
(c) N = m(g−a) = 65(7.8) = 507 N
(d) 0.80 × 637 = 509.6 N = m(g−a) → a = 9.8−509.6/65 = 1.96 m/s² downward
    (The velocity doesn't matter; only acceleration affects scale reading)
(e) N=0: m(g−a)=0 → a=g=9.8 m/s² downward (free fall)
FRQ 5

Multi-Block System

Three blocks on frictionless table: A (2 kg), B (3 kg), C (5 kg) in line, pushed by F=30 N.

(a) System acceleration. (b) Force between A and B. (c) Force between B and C. (d) Redesign: F pushes from C's side. Do answers change? Explain.

Show worked answer

Answer:

(a) a = F/total mass = 30/10 = 3 m/s²

(b) F pushes A. Force on B from A = mass of (B+C) × a = 8 × 3 = 24 N

(c) Force on C from B = mass of C × a = 5 × 3 = 15 N

(d) Same acceleration (system unchanged).
    Force between B and C: now force on A+B from C = 5×3=15 N... 
    Actually: F_AC = (m_A+m_B) × a = 5×3=15 N
    Force between A and B: F_AB = m_A × a = 2×3 = 6 N
    The contact forces are different! Largest contact force is always at the pushed end.
FRQ 6

Modified Atwood with Friction

Mass A (6 kg) on rough surface (μₖ=0.3) connected to hanging Mass B (4 kg).

(a) Find acceleration if B descends. (b) Find tension. (c) Find minimum mass of B to start motion (μₛ=0.4). (d) If system starts from rest, find speed after 2 m descent.

Show worked answer

Answer:

(a) N = m_A g = 6(9.8) = 58.8 N; fₖ = 0.3(58.8) = 17.64 N
    Net force = m_B g − fₖ = 4(9.8) − 17.64 = 39.2 − 17.64 = 21.56 N
    a = 21.56/(6+4) = 2.156 m/s²

(b) T = m_A(a+μₖg) = 6(2.156+2.94) = 6(5.096) = 30.6 N
    Check: T = m_B(g−a) = 4(9.8−2.156) = 4(7.64) = 30.6 N ✓

(c) m_B g = μₛ m_A g → m_B = μₛ m_A = 0.4(6) = 2.4 kg

(d) v² = 2ad = 2(2.156)(2) = 8.624 → v = 2.94 m/s
FRQ 7

Friction Investigation

A student slides blocks of different masses across a surface, measuring acceleration with different forces.

Mass (kg)Applied Force (N)Acceleration (m/s²)
2103.0
2155.5
4100.5
4203.0

(a) Find μₖ from the 2 kg trials. (b) Find μₖ from the 4 kg trials. (c) Are they consistent? What does this tell you about friction? (d) Predict acceleration for 3 kg block with 18 N applied force.

Show worked answer

Answer:

(a) From 2 kg, F=10 N, a=3 m/s²:
    fₖ = F − ma = 10 − 2(3) = 4 N
    μₖ = fₖ/(mg) = 4/(2×9.8) = 0.204
    
    From 2 kg, F=15 N, a=5.5 m/s²:
    fₖ = 15 − 2(5.5) = 4 N → μₖ = 0.204 ✓

(b) From 4 kg, F=10 N, a=0.5 m/s²:
    fₖ = 10 − 4(0.5) = 8 N
    μₖ = 8/(4×9.8) = 0.204

(c) Consistent! μₖ ≈ 0.204 regardless of mass or force.
    This confirms friction depends on μ and N only, not area or applied force.

(d) fₖ = μₖmg = 0.204(3)(9.8) = 5.99 N
    a = (F−fₖ)/m = (18−5.99)/3 = 12.01/3 = 4.0 m/s²
FRQ 8

Qualitative Dynamics Reasoning

A book (B) sits on top of a table (T) which sits on the floor (F).

(a) Identify all Newton's 3rd Law pairs. (b) What forces act on the table? (c) The table is accelerated upward at 2 m/s². How do forces on the book change? (d) At what acceleration would the book and table separate?

Show worked answer

Answer:

(a) 3rd Law pairs:
    - Earth pulls book down ↔ Book pulls Earth up (gravitational)
    - Table pushes book up ↔ Book pushes table down (normal contact)
    - Earth pulls table down ↔ Table pulls Earth up (gravitational)
    - Floor pushes table up ↔ Table pushes floor down (normal contact)

(b) Forces on table:
    - Weight of table (mg_T) down
    - Normal from floor (N_floor) up
    - Weight of book pressing down (reaction to table's normal on book)

(c) Book accelerates up at 2 m/s²:
    N_table_on_book = m_book(g+a) = m_book(11.8 m/s²) > m_book(g)
    Normal force on book INCREASES.

(d) Book separates when N = 0:
    m_book(g+a) = 0 → impossible for upward acceleration.
    Separation if table accelerates DOWNWARD faster than g:
    a_down > g → free fall or beyond
FRQ 9

Variable Mass System

A rocket of initial mass M₀ = 500 kg burns fuel at rate ṁ = 5 kg/s producing thrust F_thrust = 8000 N. (AP-C level)

(a) Initial acceleration of rocket. (b) Mass after 30 s. (c) Acceleration after 30 s. (d) Write equation for acceleration as function of time.

Show worked answer

Answer:

(a) Net force = Thrust − Weight = 8000 − 500(9.8) = 8000 − 4900 = 3100 N
    a₀ = F/M₀ = 3100/500 = 6.2 m/s²

(b) M(30) = 500 − 5(30) = 500 − 150 = 350 kg

(c) Net force = 8000 − 350(9.8) = 8000 − 3430 = 4570 N
    a(30) = 4570/350 = 13.1 m/s²

(d) M(t) = 500 − 5t
    a(t) = [8000 − (500−5t)(9.8)] / (500−5t)
    a(t) = 8000/(500−5t) − 9.8
FRQ 10

Synthesis: Two-Object System with Friction

Block P (3 kg) sits on top of Block Q (5 kg) on a smooth floor. Between P and Q: μₛ=0.4, μₖ=0.3.

(a) Find max force F (applied to Q) so P doesn't slip on Q. (b) If F=40 N, find acceleration of each block. (c) Find friction force on P from Q when F=40 N. (d) Find friction force on Q from P when F=40 N.

Show worked answer

Answer:

(a) Max friction on P from Q: fₛ_max = μₛ m_P g = 0.4(3)(9.8) = 11.76 N
    Max acceleration of P: a_max = fₛ_max/m_P = 11.76/3 = 3.92 m/s²
    For system to move together: a = F/(m_P+m_Q) ≤ 3.92 m/s²
    F_max = 3.92 × 8 = 31.4 N

(b) F=40 N > 31.4 N → blocks slip.
    Friction between P and Q = μₖ m_P g = 0.3(3)(9.8) = 8.82 N
    
    P: fₖ = m_P a_P → a_P = 8.82/3 = 2.94 m/s²
    Q: F − fₖ = m_Q a_Q → a_Q = (40−8.82)/5 = 31.18/5 = 6.24 m/s²

(c) Friction on P from Q = 8.82 N forward (kinetic, Q slides forward relative to P)

(d) By Newton's 3rd Law: friction on Q from P = 8.82 N backward
    (P slides backward relative to Q, so P's friction on Q is backward)

AP Physics 1 | Georgia Standards of Excellence

3.1

Work Done by a Force

The concept of work in physics is far more precise than its everyday usage. In mechanics, work is done on an object only when a force has a component along the direction of the object's displacement. Pushing against a wall with all your strength does zero work if the wall does not move. This precision is not pedantic — it is essential because work is the mechanism by which forces transfer energy into or out of an object.

Mathematically, work is the dot product of force and displacement: W = F · d = Fd cosθ, where θ is the angle between the force vector and the displacement vector. The dot product extracts only the component of force parallel to the motion. Forces perpendicular to the motion (like the normal force on a horizontally sliding block) do zero work. Forces antiparallel to motion (like kinetic friction) do negative work — they remove energy from the object.

Variable force — the integral definition: When force varies with position (as with a spring), the work must be computed as an integral: W = ∫F(x) dx. Graphically, this is the area under the Force-versus-position graph. For a spring with spring constant k compressed or stretched by distance x from equilibrium: W_spring = ½kx². This result will reappear as elastic potential energy in the next section.

Net work: The net work on an object is the algebraic sum of the work done by every individual force. This equals the work done by the net force: W_net = (ΣF) · d = (ΣF)d cosθ.

WORK (constant force):
  W = F · d · cosθ         [Joules, J = N·m]
  θ = angle between force vector and displacement vector

  θ = 0°:   W = Fd   (force parallel to motion → positive work)
  θ = 90°:  W = 0    (force perpendicular to motion → zero work)
  θ = 180°: W = −Fd  (force opposing motion → negative work)

WORK (variable force — spring, stretched by x):
  W_spring = ∫₀ˣ kx' dx' = ½kx²    [J]
  (= area under F vs. x graph)
3.2

Kinetic Energy and the Work-Energy Theorem

Kinetic energy (KE) is the energy an object possesses by virtue of its motion. It is a scalar defined as KE = ½mv². Because it involves v², kinetic energy is always non-negative, and doubling the speed quadruples the kinetic energy — a crucial insight for understanding why high-speed collisions and car crashes are so much more destructive than low-speed ones.

The Work-Energy Theorem is one of the most powerful statements in classical mechanics: the net work done on an object equals the change in its kinetic energy. This is derived directly from Newton's Second Law (F = ma) by integrating over displacement, so it is not an independent law — it is Newton's Second Law in energy language. Its power is that all the vector complexity of force analysis collapses into a single scalar energy-bookkeeping equation.

Applying the work-energy theorem: if you know the net work done on an object, you immediately know how much its kinetic energy changed. This often provides a faster route to an answer than the kinematic equations, especially when multiple forces act along curved paths where direction changes continuously.

KINETIC ENERGY:
  KE = ½mv²         [Joules, J]
  KE ≥ 0 always (scalar)
  If v doubles → KE quadruples

WORK-ENERGY THEOREM:
  W_net = ΔKE = ½mv_f² − ½mv_i²
  
  Derivation: F = ma, use v² = v₀² + 2aΔx
  → FΔx = ½mv² − ½mv₀²  ✓

Solving for final speed:
  v_f = √(v_i² + 2W_net/m)
3.3

Potential Energy and Conservative Forces

Not all work done on an object is permanently "gone" — some of it can be stored and later recovered as kinetic energy. This recoverable stored energy is called potential energy. It is associated with the configuration of a system — specifically, the relative positions of objects interacting through a conservative force.

A conservative force is one for which the work done depends only on the initial and final positions, not on the path taken between them. Equivalently, the work done by a conservative force around any closed loop is zero. Gravity and the spring force are both conservative. Kinetic friction is not — it dissipates more energy along a longer path, so the work done depends on path length.

For any conservative force, we define a potential energy function U such that the work done by the force equals the negative of the change in potential energy: W_conservative = −ΔU. The gravitational potential energy near Earth's surface is U_g = mgy (where y is height above a chosen reference). The elastic potential energy stored in a spring is U_spring = ½kx². Only changes in potential energy ΔU are physically meaningful — the choice of reference level (where U = 0) is arbitrary.

CONSERVATIVE FORCE:
  W_conservative = −ΔU    (path-independent)

GRAVITATIONAL POTENTIAL ENERGY (near Earth):
  U_g = mgy               [J]
  ΔU_g = mgΔy = mg(y_f − y_i)
  (choose reference y=0 wherever convenient)

ELASTIC POTENTIAL ENERGY (spring):
  U_spring = ½kx²         [J]
  x = displacement from natural (equilibrium) length
3.4

Conservation of Mechanical Energy

When only conservative forces act on a system, the sum of kinetic and potential energies — called the total mechanical energy — remains constant throughout the motion. This is the law of conservation of mechanical energy: E_mech = KE + U = constant. It transforms complicated force and trajectory problems into simple energy bookkeeping: wherever you are in the motion, E_mech is the same value.

In practice: KE_i + U_i = KE_f + U_f, or ½mv_i² + U_i = ½mv_f² + U_f. You can pick any two points in the motion, equate their total mechanical energies, and solve for the unknown. The power of this approach is that the path between the two points is completely irrelevant — only the initial and final states matter.

When energy is not conserved: If non-conservative forces like kinetic friction or air resistance do work, mechanical energy decreases (is converted to thermal energy). We account for this as: E_f = E_i + W_nc. Since friction always does negative work (removes mechanical energy), W_nc is negative whenever friction acts, and E_f < E_i.

CONSERVATION OF MECHANICAL ENERGY (no friction):
  E_mech = KE + PE = constant
  ½mv_i² + U_i = ½mv_f² + U_f

For gravity (U = mgy):
  ½mv_i² + mgy_i = ½mv_f² + mgy_f

WITH NON-CONSERVATIVE FORCES (e.g., friction):
  E_f = E_i + W_nc
  ½mv_f² + mgy_f = ½mv_i² + mgy_i + W_friction
  W_friction = −fₖd  (always negative → energy lost to heat)
3.5

Power

Power is the rate at which work is done, or equivalently, the rate at which energy is transferred or transformed. The same amount of work can be done quickly (high power) or slowly (low power). A weightlifter who lifts 100 kg by 2 m does the same work as an escalator carrying the same load the same height — but the weightlifter does it in 2 seconds while the escalator takes 20 seconds, so the weightlifter operates at ten times the power.

The SI unit of power is the Watt (W): 1 W = 1 J/s. Average power over a time interval is P_avg = W/Δt. Instantaneous power — the power at a single moment — is P = dW/dt = F · v = Fv cosθ. This form is particularly useful for analyzing engines and motors, where force may be constant but speed varies.

POWER:
  P_avg = W/Δt = ΔE/Δt    [Watts, W = J/s]
  P_inst = F · v = Fv cosθ [W]

Unit conversions:
  1 hp (horsepower) = 746 W
  1 kW = 1000 W

Common applications:
  Engine at constant speed: P = F_drive × v
    (ΣF = 0 at constant v → F_drive = F_drag; P = F_drag × v)
  Pumping fluid to height h at volume rate Q:
    P = ρgQh   (ρ = fluid density, Q = m³/s)
3.1

Work as Area Under F-x Graph

When force varies with position, work = area under the F vs. x curve. For a constant force, it is a rectangle (W = Fd). For a spring (F = kx), it is a triangle (W = ½kx²). This is the geometric interpretation of W = ∫F dx.

Text version of this diagram
F (N)
│           ●  Spring: F = kx
│          /│
│         / │   Area = ½ × base × height
│        /  │       = ½ × x₀ × kx₀ = ½kx₀²
│       /   │       = elastic PE stored in spring
│      /    │
│     /     │
│    /      │
└───/───────┼────── x (m)
   0        x₀

Constant force (horizontal line): rectangle → W = F·d
Spring (rising line):              triangle → W = ½kx²
General curve: W = ∫F dx = area under curve (positive or negative)
3.2

Energy Bar Charts: Conservation Tracking

Energy bar charts show how total mechanical energy is distributed at different points. Total bar height stays constant when no non-conservative forces act. Friction converts mechanical energy to thermal energy (heat).

Text version of this diagram
Ball dropped from height h — three positions:

Position A (top, at rest):     Position B (midway):     Position C (bottom):
│ PE │                         │PE│                     │   │
│    │                         │  │KE│                  │   │   │KE│
│    │                         │  │  │                  │   │   │  │
└────┘                         └──┴──┘                  └───┴───┴──┘
  ½kA²=0 + mgh₀                   half PE, half KE          all KE = mgh₀
                       
With friction (sliding down incline):
│PE │ →  │KE│PE│  →  │KE│PE│Th│
           (thermal bar grows as KE+PE decreases)
Total: KE + PE + Thermal = constant (energy conserved)
3.3

Power: Slope of Energy vs. Time

Power is the rate of energy transfer. Steeper slope on an E-t graph means higher power. For an object moving at speed v against a force F, instantaneous power P = Fv cosθ.

Text version of this diagram
Energy (J)
│                   / ← high power agent (steep slope)
│                  /
│              ───/  ← low power agent (shallow slope)
│          ───/
│      ───/
│  ───/
└──────────────────────────── t (s)

P_avg = ΔE/Δt = total work / total time

Engine maintaining constant speed v against drag force Fd:
  ΣF = 0 → F_engine = F_drag
  P = F_engine × v = F_drag × v

Converting: 1 hp = 746 W = 746 J/s
Example 3.1

Work by a Constant Force

Algebraic Calculation

Question: A 50 N force at 37° above horizontal pushes a box 8 m. Find work done.

Show solution

Solution:

W = Fd cosθ = 50(8)(cos37°) = 50(8)(0.8) = 320 J
Example 3.2

Work-Energy Theorem

Algebraic Calculation

Question: A 4 kg box starts at rest. Net force 20 N acts over 5 m. Find final speed.

Show solution

Solution:

W_net = F·d = 20(5) = 100 J
W_net = ΔKE = ½mv² − 0
100 = ½(4)v²
v² = 50
v = 7.07 m/s
Example 3.3

Energy Conservation: Falling

Algebraic Calculation

Question: Ball dropped from 20 m. Find speed at 5 m above ground.

Show solution

Solution:

E conserved: mgh₁ = mgh₂ + ½mv²
g(20) = g(5) + ½v²
9.8(15) = ½v²
v² = 294
v = 17.1 m/s
Example 3.4

Spring Energy

Algebraic Calculation

Question: Spring (k=500 N/m) compressed 0.2 m launches 0.5 kg ball horizontally. Find launch speed.

Show solution

Solution:

PE_spring = ½kx² = ½(500)(0.04) = 10 J
½mv² = 10
v² = 40
v = 6.32 m/s
Example 3.5

Power Calculation

Algebraic Calculation

Question: A 70 kg person climbs 20 m stairs in 30 s. Find average power output.

Show solution

Solution:

W = mgh = 70(9.8)(20) = 13720 J
P = W/t = 13720/30 = 457 W (about 0.61 hp)
Example 3.6

Friction and Energy Loss

Algebraic Calculation

Question: A 3 kg block slides 4 m down a 30° incline with μₖ=0.

  1. Find (a) work by gravity, (b) work by friction, (c) final KE if starting from rest.
Show solution

Solution:

Height fallen: h = 4 sin30° = 2 m
(a) W_gravity = mgh = 3(9.8)(2) = 58.8 J

(b) N = mg cos30° = 3(9.8)(0.866) = 25.5 N
    fₖ = μₖN = 0.20(25.5) = 5.1 N
    W_friction = −fₖd = −5.1(4) = −20.4 J

(c) KE_f = W_net = W_gravity + W_friction = 58.8 − 20.4 = 38.4 J
    Check: ½mv² = 38.4 → v = √(25.6) = 5.06 m/s
Example 3.7

Energy at Multiple Points

Algebraic Calculation

Question: A 2 kg ball is thrown upward at 15 m/s from ground. Find KE and PE at h=5 m. (No friction)

Show solution

Solution:

Initial KE = ½(2)(225) = 225 J
Initial PE = 0

At h=5 m (conservation):
PE = mgh = 2(9.8)(5) = 98 J
KE = 225 − 98 = 127 J
v = √(2×127/2) = √127 = 11.3 m/s
Example 3.8

Power from Force and Velocity

Algebraic Calculation

Question: A car engine applies 3000 N at 25 m/s. What is the power output in watts and horsepower?

Show solution

Solution:

P = Fv = 3000 × 25 = 75,000 W = 75 kW
hp = 75000/746 = 100.5 hp
Example 3.9

Variable Force Work (AP-C)

Calculus Derivation

Question: F(x) = (3x² + 2x) N. Find work from x=0 to x=3 m.

Show solution

Solution:

W = ∫₀³ (3x² + 2x) dx = [x³ + x²]₀³ = (27 + 9) − 0 = 36 J
Example 3.10

Conservation with Spring

Algebraic Calculation

Question: A 1 kg block compresses spring (k=800 N/m) by 0.15 m. Spring releases block on frictionless floor. Find max speed.

Show solution

Solution:

½kx² = ½mv²
½(800)(0.0225) = ½(1)v²
9 = ½v²
v = √18 = 4.24 m/s
Example 3.11

Roller Coaster Loop

Algebraic Calculation

Question: A car at top of 40 m high hill enters a loop of radius 12 m. What is minimum speed at loop top? Height of loop top = 24 m.

Show solution

Solution:

At loop top: minimum speed when N=0 → v_top = √(gr) = √(9.8×12) = 10.8 m/s

Energy conservation (hill top to loop top):
½mv₀² + mgh₁ = ½mv_top² + mgh₂
v₀² + 2g(h₁) = v_top² + 2g(h₂)
v₀² = v_top² + 2g(h₂ − h₁) = 116.6 + 2(9.8)(24−40) = 116.6 − 313.6 → negative
This means: need only enough speed at hill top to maintain contact at loop.
v₀_min at hill top: ½mv₀² + mg(40) = ½m(gr) + mg(24)
v₀² = gr + 2g(24−40) = gr − 32g = g(r−32) = 9.8(12−32) < 0
→ Starting height of 40 m is more than sufficient.
Example 3.12

Hooke's Law & Energy

Algebraic Calculation

Question: Two identical springs (k=300 N/m each). (a) What is total PE if both compressed 0.1 m? (b) If in parallel (same compression)?

Show solution

Solution:

(a) Each: PE = ½(300)(0.01) = 1.5 J. Total = 3 J
(b) Parallel springs: k_eff = 600 N/m, x = 0.1 m
    PE = ½(600)(0.01) = 3 J (same!)
    
    If in series: k_eff = 150 N/m, same force F=kx shared
Example 3.13

Energy Lost to Friction

Algebraic Calculation

Question: Block slides 6 m across floor and decelerates from 8 m/s to 3 m/s. Mass = 2 kg. Find μₖ.

Show solution

Solution:

Energy lost = ΔKE = ½m(v₀² − v²) = ½(2)(64−9) = 55 J
W_friction = fₖ × d = μₖmg × d = 55
μₖ = 55/(2 × 9.8 × 6) = 55/117.6 = 0.468
Example 3.14

Efficiency

Algebraic Calculation

Question: A motor (1500 W) lifts a 200 kg load 10 m. It takes 20 s. Find efficiency.

Show solution

Solution:

Useful work done = mgh = 200(9.8)(10) = 19600 J
Energy input = P × t = 1500 × 20 = 30000 J
Efficiency = (19600/30000) × 100% = 65.3%
Example 3.15

Escape from Gravity (PE → KE)

Algebraic Calculation

Question: Ball launched from ground at 15 m/s. What is its height when speed = 10 m/s? (No friction)

Show solution

Solution:

½mv₀² = ½mv² + mgh
½(225) = ½(100) + 9.8h
112.5 = 50 + 9.8h
h = 62.5/9.8 = 6.38 m
Example 3.16

Power and Velocity of Car

Algebraic Calculation

Question: Car engine provides constant power 60 kW. Mass = 1200 kg. At what speed does the car reach maximum velocity (when driving force equals friction = 800 N)?

Show solution

Solution:

P = Fv at constant speed
60000 = 800 × v
v = 75 m/s = 270 km/h
Example 3.17

Pendulum Energy

Algebraic Calculation

Question: A 0.5 kg pendulum bob swings from 0.3 m above lowest point. Find (a) max speed, (b) speed at 0.1 m above lowest point.

Show solution

Solution:

(a) All PE → KE at bottom:
    mgh = ½mv²
    v = √(2gh) = √(2×9.8×0.3) = √5.88 = 2.42 m/s

(b) At h=0.1 m:
    mgh₀ = mgh + ½mv²
    v = √(2g(h₀−h)) = √(2×9.8×0.2) = √3.92 = 1.98 m/s
Example 3.18

Spring Launched Projectile

Algebraic Calculation

Question: Spring (k=400 N/m, compressed 0.25 m) launches 0.2 kg ball at 30° above horizontal. Find range. (g=9.8 m/s²)

Show solution

Solution:

PE_spring = ½(400)(0.0625) = 12.5 J = ½mv²
v₀ = √(2×12.5/0.2) = √125 = 11.18 m/s

v₀ₓ = 11.18 cos30° = 9.68 m/s
v₀ᵧ = 11.18 sin30° = 5.59 m/s
T = 2v₀ᵧ/g = 1.14 s
R = v₀ₓ × T = 9.68 × 1.14 = 11.0 m
Example 3.19

Energy Theorem with Calculus

Calculus Derivation

Question: F(x) = (10 − 2x) N acts on 2 kg object at rest. Find speed at x=4 m.

Show solution

Solution:

W = ∫₀⁴ (10 − 2x) dx = [10x − x²]₀⁴ = 40 − 16 = 24 J
W = ΔKE = ½mv² − 0
24 = ½(2)v²
v = √24 = 4.90 m/s
Example 3.20

AP FRQ: Complete Energy Analysis

Free Response

Question: A 5 kg block starts from rest at top of ramp (h=4 m, length=8 m, μₖ=0.15). (a) Find speed at bottom using energy methods. (b) Block then slides on flat floor and compresses a spring (k=600 N/m). How far is spring compressed? (c) Does block return to original height? Justify. (d) Sketch energy bar charts at each stage.

Show solution

Solution:

(a) On ramp:
    W_friction = −μₖmg cosθ × L = −0.15(5)(9.8)(cos30°)(8)
    cos θ = h/L → sinθ = 4/8 = 0.5, θ=30°, cosθ=0.866
    W_friction = −0.15(5)(9.8)(0.866)(8) = −50.9 J
    
    E_initial = mgh = 5(9.8)(4) = 196 J
    KE_bottom = 196 − 50.9 = 145.1 J
    v = √(2×145.1/5) = √58.04 = 7.62 m/s

(b) On flat floor with spring (assuming frictionless floor):
    ½mv² = ½kx²
    145.1 = ½(600)x²
    x² = 290.2/600 = 0.484
    x = 0.695 m

(c) No. Energy was lost to friction on the ramp. Even if spring and floor are frictionless,
    block returns with only 145.1 J (not 196 J), which brings it only to h=145.1/(mg)=2.97 m
    (not original 4 m).

(d) Energy bars:
    Initial: [====large====] PE, [empty] KE, [empty] Spring PE
    Bottom of ramp: [=====] KE, [empty] PE, [empty] Spring PE (some lost to heat)
    Max spring: [empty] KE, [empty] PE, [=====] Spring PE
