AP Physics 2 & C | Georgia Standards of Excellence

12.1

Magnetic Fields and the Lorentz Force on Moving Charges

Magnetism and electricity are two manifestations of a single underlying electromagnetic force. Magnetic fields are created by moving charges (electric currents) and by quantum spin (permanent magnets). The SI unit of magnetic field strength B is the Tesla (T): 1 T = 1 N/(A·m). Earth's magnetic field is about 50 μT; a strong research magnet reaches 10–20 T; a clinical MRI machine uses 1.5–3 T.

The magnetic force on a moving charge is the Lorentz force: F = qv × B. The magnitude is |F| = qvB sinθ, where θ is the angle between the velocity v and the magnetic field B. Three critical properties distinguish the magnetic force from electric and gravitational forces: (1) it acts only on moving charges, not stationary ones; (2) it is always perpendicular to both v and B; and (3) because it is perpendicular to v, it does no work — it can change the direction of motion but never the speed or kinetic energy.

The direction follows the right-hand rule: point fingers of your right hand in the direction of v, curl them toward B — the extended thumb points in the direction of F for a positive charge. For a negative charge, the force is reversed.

Circular motion in a uniform field: Since the magnetic force is always perpendicular to v, it acts as a centripetal force for a charge moving perpendicular to B. Setting qvB = mv²/r gives the cyclotron radius r = mv/(qB). The period T = 2πm/(qB) and cyclotron frequency f = qB/(2πm) are independent of the particle's speed — the basis of the cyclotron particle accelerator.

LORENTZ FORCE:
  F = qv × B          (vector cross product)
  |F| = qvB sinθ      [N]
  Direction: right-hand rule (reversed for negative charges)
  
  KEY PROPERTIES:
  • Acts only on MOVING charges (not stationary)
  • Always ⊥ to v → does NO work → KE unchanged
  • Changes direction of velocity, not speed

CIRCULAR MOTION IN UNIFORM B (v ⊥ B):
  qvB = mv²/r  → r = mv/(qB)      [cyclotron radius]
  T = 2πm/(qB)                     [period, speed-independent!]
  f = qB/(2πm)                     [cyclotron frequency]
12.2

Magnetic Force on Current-Carrying Conductors

A current-carrying wire placed in a magnetic field experiences a force because the wire contains moving charges (the current), and each moving charge feels the Lorentz force. For a straight wire of length L carrying current I in a magnetic field B, the force is F = IL × B, with magnitude F = BIL sinθ (θ = angle between wire direction and B).

Two parallel wires carrying currents in the same direction attract each other; opposite-direction currents repel. This force between parallel wires historically provided the definition of the Ampere: 1 A is the current that produces 2 × 10⁻⁷ N of force per meter of length between two infinitely long parallel wires 1 m apart.

A current loop in a magnetic field experiences a torque that tends to align the loop's magnetic moment with the external field. The magnetic moment is μ = NIA (N turns, area A, current I). The torque is τ = NIABsinθ = μ × B. This torque-on-a-loop principle is the basis of all electric motors and galvanometers.

FORCE ON CURRENT-CARRYING WIRE:
  F = IL × B       (vector form)
  |F| = BIL sinθ   [N]
  Direction: right-hand rule with current direction replacing v

TORQUE ON CURRENT LOOP:
  τ = NIAB sinθ    [N·m]
  μ = NIA          (magnetic moment [A·m²])
  Equilibrium: θ = 0° (μ ∥ B)
  Maximum torque: θ = 90° (μ ⊥ B)
12.3

Sources of Magnetic Fields

The Biot-Savart Law states that a small current element I dl creates a magnetic field dB = (μ₀/4π)(I dl × r̂)/r² at a point at displacement r from the element. Here μ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ T·m/A is the permeability of free space. Integrating over a complete circuit gives the total field. Key results: the field at the center of a circular loop of radius R is B = μ₀I/(2R); the field inside a solenoid of n turns per unit length is B = μ₀nI (uniform, directed along the axis).

Ampere's Law is the magnetic analog of Gauss's Law for electric fields. It states: ∮B·dl = μ₀I_enc — the line integral of B around any closed path equals μ₀ times the total current enclosed. For highly symmetric configurations, this provides an elegant shortcut that avoids the Biot-Savart integration.

KEY MAGNETIC FIELDS (from Biot-Savart or Ampere's Law):
  Long straight wire (distance r):   B = μ₀I/(2πr)
  Center of circular loop (radius R): B = μ₀I/(2R)
  Solenoid interior (n turns/length): B = μ₀nI = μ₀NI/L
  Toroid (N turns, radius r):         B = μ₀NI/(2πr)

  μ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ T·m/A

AMPERE'S LAW:
  ∮B·dl = μ₀I_enc   (for steady currents)
12.4

Faraday's Law and Electromagnetic Induction

Faraday's Law of Electromagnetic Induction: A changing magnetic flux through a conducting loop induces an EMF in the loop: ε = −dΦ_B/dt. The magnetic flux through a surface is Φ_B = ∫B·dA = BA cosθ (for uniform B). The induced EMF drives a current in the loop (if the loop is a closed conductor), which then dissipates energy in the circuit's resistance.

Lenz's Law is encoded in the negative sign: the induced current always flows in such a direction as to oppose the change in magnetic flux that caused it. If the flux is increasing through a loop, the induced current creates a field opposing the increase. If flux is decreasing, the induced current creates a field to maintain it. This is energy conservation in disguise — if induced currents aided the change in flux, we could extract unlimited energy from a system.

Faraday's Law is the operating principle behind generators (mechanical rotation → changing flux → EMF), transformers (changing current in primary coil → changing flux → EMF in secondary coil), induction cooktops, and eddy-current braking. It is one of Maxwell's four equations that unify all of electromagnetism.

MAGNETIC FLUX:
  Φ_B = B·A = BA cosθ    [Webers, Wb = T·m²]
  θ = angle between B and the area's normal vector

FARADAY'S LAW:
  ε = −dΦ_B/dt = −N dΦ/dt   [V]  (N = number of turns)
  
LENZ'S LAW (the minus sign):
  Induced current opposes the CHANGE in flux (energy conservation)
  Flux increasing → induced current creates opposing B
  Flux decreasing → induced current creates sustaining B

MOTIONAL EMF (conductor of length L moving at v in field B):
  ε = BLv   (when B, L, v all mutually perpendicular)

TRANSFORMERS (ideal):
  V_s/V_p = N_s/N_p    (voltage ratio = turns ratio)
  I_s/I_p = N_p/N_s    (currents are inverse of turns ratio)
  Power: V_p I_p = V_s I_s   (100% efficient ideal transformer)
12.1

Right-Hand Rules for Magnetic Fields and Forces

Two key right-hand rules: (1) curl fingers around a wire in the direction of current → fingers show B field direction (circular). (2) Point fingers in v direction, curl toward B → thumb gives F direction for positive charge.

Text version of this diagram
RHR 1 — FIELD AROUND CURRENT-CARRYING WIRE:
  Thumb = current direction (I)
  Fingers curl = B field direction (circles)

  Current I OUT of page (⊙):
  ← B above (leftward)
  ● (wire)
  → B below (rightward)
  B forms CCW circles (viewed from current direction)

RHR 2 — FORCE ON MOVING CHARGE (F = qv × B):
  Step 1: Point fingers flat in direction of v
  Step 2: Curl fingers toward B
  Step 3: Thumb = direction of F (for positive charge)
  
  Example: v = → (east), B = ↑ (north):
    F = qv × B = q(east × north) = q(UP) ← out of ground!
    
  For NEGATIVE charge: reverse the direction of F
12.2

Magnetic Fields from Common Geometries

The Biot-Savart Law and Ampere's Law give the field for specific current geometries. The solenoid is the most important: uniform field inside, nearly zero outside — the magnetic analog of a parallel-plate capacitor.

Text version of this diagram
LONG STRAIGHT WIRE (distance r):
  B = μ₀I/(2πr)    [circles around wire]
  Closer to wire → stronger B (1/r relationship)

CIRCULAR LOOP (radius R, at center):
  B = μ₀I/(2R)     [perpendicular to plane of loop]

SOLENOID (n turns per meter, length L >> radius):
  B_inside = μ₀nI = μ₀NI/L   [uniform, parallel to axis]
  B_outside ≈ 0                [fields cancel outside]

  Cross-section:
  ─────────────────────────────
  ) ) ) ) ) ) ) ) ) ) ) ) ) ) )   coil turns
  ←←←←←←←←←← B field inside ←←←←←←←←←←
  ) ) ) ) ) ) ) ) ) ) ) ) ) ) )
  ─────────────────────────────

μ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ T·m/A (permeability of free space)
12.3

Electromagnetic Induction and Lenz's Law

Changing magnetic flux through a loop induces an EMF (Faraday's Law). The induced current direction (Lenz's Law) always opposes the change — if flux increases, induced current creates field to oppose the increase.

Text version of this diagram
Φ_B = BA cosθ  [Webers, Wb]    ε = −dΦ/dt  [Volts]

CASE 1: Bar magnet N-pole approaching loop (B into page increasing):
  
  Increasing ⊗ flux:
  ┌──────────────────┐   Induced current: COUNTERCLOCKWISE
  │  ⊗  ⊗  ⊗  ⊗  ⊗ │   (creates ⊙ field inside to oppose ⊗ increase)
  │  ⊗  ⊗  ⊗  ⊗  ⊗ │   
  │                  │←→ N-pole of magnet approaching
  └──────────────────┘

CASE 2: Magnet receding (B into page decreasing):
  Induced current: CLOCKWISE (creates ⊗ to maintain decreasing flux)

MOTIONAL EMF (wire moving in B field):
  B ⊗, length L, velocity v →:
  ε = BLv   (free charges in wire feel F = qv×B, separate to ends)
Example 12.1

Force on Moving Charge

Q: Proton (q=1.6×10⁻¹⁹ C) moving at 3×10⁶ m/s perpendicular to B=0.5T. Find force.

Show solution
F = qvB sinθ = (1.6×10⁻¹⁹)(3×10⁶)(0.5)(1) = 2.4×10⁻¹³ N
Example 12.2

Circular Radius in B-Field

Q: Electron (m=9.1×10⁻³¹ kg, q=1.6×10⁻¹⁹ C) at 2×10⁷ m/s enters B=0.01T. Find radius.

Show solution
r = mv/(qB) = (9.1×10⁻³¹)(2×10⁷)/((1.6×10⁻¹⁹)(0.01))
r = 1.82×10⁻²³/1.6×10⁻²¹ = 0.01138 m = 11.4 mm
Example 12.3

Force on Wire

Q: 0.5 m wire carrying 4 A in B=0.3T perpendicular to wire. Force?

Show solution
F = ILB sinθ = 4(0.5)(0.3)(1) = 0.6 N
Example 12.4

Magnetic Field of Wire

Q: B at r=0.05 m from long wire carrying I=10 A.

Show solution
B = μ₀I/(2πr) = (4π×10⁻⁷)(10)/(2π×0.05) = 4π×10⁻⁶/0.1π = 4×10⁻⁵ T = 40 μT
Example 12.5

Solenoid Field

Q: Solenoid: 500 turns, L=0.25 m, I=3A. Find B inside.

Show solution
n = 500/0.25 = 2000 turns/m
B = μ₀nI = (4π×10⁻⁷)(2000)(3) = 2.4π×10⁻³ = 7.54×10⁻³ T = 7.54 mT
Example 12.6

Magnetic Flux

Q: 0.05 m² coil at 30° to B=0.8T. Flux?

Show solution
Φ = BA cosθ = 0.8(0.05)cos30° = 0.04(0.866) = 0.0346 Wb
Note: θ is angle between B and normal to surface.
At 30° to surface means 60° to normal: Φ = 0.8(0.05)cos60° = 0.02 Wb
Example 12.7

Faraday's Law: EMF

Q: 200-turn coil, area 0.03 m². B changes from 0.1T to 0.5T in 0.04 s. Find ε.

Show solution
ε = −N × ΔΦ/Δt = −N × A × ΔB/Δt
ε = 200 × 0.03 × (0.5−0.1)/0.04 = 200 × 0.03 × 10 = 60 V
Example 12.8

Motional EMF

Q: 0.4 m bar moves at 5 m/s perpendicular to B=0.6T. EMF?

Show solution
ε = BLv = 0.6(0.4)(5) = 1.2 V
Example 12.9

Lenz's Law Direction

Q: Circular loop in xy-plane. B (in z-direction) increasing. What is current direction?

Show solution
Increasing B (upward, through loop) → Lenz says oppose increase
Induced current creates B opposing (downward inside loop)
By RHR: current flows CLOCKWISE when viewed from +z direction.
Example 12.10

Velocity Selector

Q: E=5000 V/m, B=0.02T in velocity selector. What speed is selected?

Show solution
v = E/B = 5000/0.02 = 250,000 m/s = 2.5×10⁵ m/s
Only particles with exactly this speed travel straight.
Example 12.11

Transformer

Q: Transformer: N_p=200, N_s=800 turns, V_p=120V. Find V_s and I ratio.

Show solution
V_s/V_p = N_s/N_p → V_s = 120(800/200) = 480 V (step-up)
I_s/I_p = N_p/N_s = 200/800 = 1/4 (current steps down)
P_in = P_out: V_p I_p = V_s I_s (ideal transformer)
Example 12.12

AC Generator EMF

Q: Coil (N=100 turns, A=0.01 m²) rotates at ω=120π rad/s in B=0.5T. Peak EMF?

Show solution
ε_max = NBAω = 100(0.5)(0.01)(120π) = 60π = 188.5 V
ε(t) = 188.5 sin(120πt) V
Example 12.13

Cyclotron Frequency

Q: Proton in B=2T cyclotron. Find frequency.

Show solution
f = qB/(2πm) = (1.6×10⁻¹⁹)(2)/(2π × 1.67×10⁻²⁷)
f = 3.2×10⁻¹⁹/(1.05×10⁻²⁶) = 3.05×10⁷ Hz = 30.5 MHz
Example 12.14

Force Between Wires

Q: Two parallel wires 0.1 m apart, I₁=5A, I₂=8A, same direction. Force per meter?

Show solution
F/L = μ₀I₁I₂/(2πd) = (4π×10⁻⁷)(5)(8)/(2π×0.1)
F/L = (4π×10⁻⁷)(40)/(0.2π) = 8×10⁻⁵ N/m (attractive, same direction)
Example 12.15

Inductor Energy (AP-C)

Q: Inductor L=50mH, I=4A. Energy stored?

Show solution
U = ½LI² = ½(0.05)(16) = 0.4 J
Example 12.16

Inductance of Solenoid

Q: Solenoid: 1000 turns, L=0.5m, radius=0.02m. Find inductance.

Show solution
n = 1000/0.5 = 2000 turns/m
A = π(0.02)² = 1.257×10⁻³ m²
L = μ₀n²Al = (4π×10⁻⁷)(4×10⁶)(1.257×10⁻³)(0.5)
L = (4π×10⁻⁷)(4×10⁶)(6.28×10⁻⁴) = (5.027×10⁻³)(6.28×10⁻⁴)×0.5 
L ≈ 1.58×10⁻³ H = 1.58 mH
Example 12.17

Mass Spectrometer

Q: Ion (q=1.6×10⁻¹⁹, m=?) enters B=0.5T at v=2×10⁵ m/s, radius=0.04m. Find mass.

Show solution
r = mv/(qB) → m = qBr/v = (1.6×10⁻¹⁹)(0.5)(0.04)/(2×10⁵)
m = 3.2×10⁻²¹/2×10⁵ = 1.6×10⁻²⁶ kg ≈ 10 amu (neon isotope)
Example 12.18

Back-EMF in Motor

Q: Motor: ε=120V, R=2Ω, I=5A when running. Back-EMF?

Show solution
V_net = ε − ε_back = IR
ε_back = ε − IR = 120 − 5(2) = 110 V
Power to motor: P = εI = 600 W
Power to heat: P = I²R = 50 W
Mechanical power out: 600 − 50 = 550 W
Example 12.19

Maxwell's Displacement Current (AP-C)

Q: Capacitor plates (A=10⁻³ m²), E changing at 10¹² V/(m·s). Find displacement current.

Show solution
I_d = ε₀ × dE/dt × A = (8.85×10⁻¹²)(10¹²)(10⁻³) = 8.85×10⁻³ A = 8.85 mA
This displacement current creates a B-field just as real current does.
Example 12.20

AP FRQ: Electromagnetic Induction

Rectangular loop (0.4 m × 0.2 m, R=5Ω) moves at 3 m/s into uniform B=0.8T (into page).

(a) EMF when leading edge enters. (b) Induced current magnitude and direction. (c) Force on leading edge. (d) Power dissipated. (e) Where does energy come from?

Show solution
(a) ε = BLv = 0.8(0.4)(3) = 0.96 V
    (L = 0.4 m = height of loop perpendicular to motion)

(b) I = ε/R = 0.96/5 = 0.192 A
    Lenz's Law: flux into page increasing → induced B out of page → CCW current

(c) F = BIL = 0.8(0.192)(0.4) = 0.0614 N (opposing motion, by Lenz)

(d) P = ε²/R = (0.96)²/5 = 0.184 W = I²R = (0.192)²(5) = 0.184 W ✓

(e) Work done by external agent pushing the loop against the retarding magnetic force.
    F_push = F_retard = 0.0614 N; P = Fv = 0.0614(3) = 0.184 W ✓

Free Response Questions (FRQ 1-10)

FRQ 1

Charged Particle in B Field

A proton (m=1.67e-27 kg, q=1.6e-19 C) enters a 0.5 T field at 90° with speed 3e6 m/s. (a) Find r. (b) Find period T. (c) Find kinetic energy. (d) Describe the path.

Show worked answer

(a) r = mv/(qB) = 1.67e-27*3e6/(1.6e-19*0.5) = 5.01e-21/8e-20 = 0.0626 m = 6.26 cm
(b) T = 2*pi*m/(qB) = 2*pi*1.67e-27/(1.6e-19*0.5) = 1.05e-26/8e-20 = 1.31e-7 s = 131 ns
(c) KE = (1/2)*mv^2 = 0.5*1.67e-27*(9e12) = 7.52e-15 J = 47 keV
(d) Circle: radius 6.26 cm in a plane perpendicular to B; magnetic force provides centripetal acceleration; speed constant (magnetic force does no work)
FRQ 2

Force on Current-Carrying Wire

A 0.3 m wire carries 5A at 60° to a 0.8 T field. (a) Force magnitude. (b) If the wire is a loop (area 0.04 m²) with 50 turns, find max torque. (c) Find the orientation for max torque.

Show worked answer

(a) F = BIL sinθ = 0.8*5*0.3*sin60 = 1.2*0.866 = 1.04 N
(b) tau_max = NIAB = 50*5*0.04*0.8 = 8 N*m
(c) Max torque when loop plane is parallel to B (magnetic moment perpendicular to B, θ=90°)
FRQ 3

Faraday's Law: EMF from Changing Area

A 200-turn coil has area expanding at 2e-3 m²/s in B=0.4 T (perpendicular to coil). (a) Find induced EMF. (b) If R=8Ω, find induced current. (c) In which direction does it flow (Lenz's Law)?

Show worked answer

(a) EMF = -N * dPhi/dt = -N*B*(dA/dt) = -200*0.4*2e-3 = -0.16V; |EMF|=0.16V
(b) I = EMF/R = 0.16/8 = 0.02 A = 20 mA
(c) Area increasing -> flux increasing (B into page, say) -> induced current opposes increase
    -> induced B must point out of page inside coil -> counterclockwise (by RHR)
FRQ 4

Transformer Calculation

A step-down transformer: Vp=220V, Vs=22V, Ns=100 turns, 90% efficient. (a) Find Np. (b) If load is 10Ω, find Is, Ip, Pp, Ps. (c) Find power wasted.

Show worked answer

(a) Np/Ns = Vp/Vs -> Np = 220/22 * 100 = 1000 turns
(b) Is = Vs/R = 22/10 = 2.2 A
    Ps = Vs*Is = 22*2.2 = 48.4 W
    Pp = Ps/efficiency = 48.4/0.9 = 53.8 W
    Ip = Pp/Vp = 53.8/220 = 0.244 A
(c) P_wasted = Pp - Ps = 53.8 - 48.4 = 5.4 W (in transformer windings and core)
FRQ 5

Mass Spectrometer

Singly-ionized ions (q=1.6e-19 C) are accelerated through 1000V and enter B=0.2T. Ions of mass 32 u and 34 u enter (1u = 1.66e-27 kg). Find (a) speed at entry, (b) radius for each ion, (c) separation on detector plate.

Show worked answer

(a) qV = (1/2)mv^2; v = sqrt(2qV/m) -- different for each mass!
    For m32: v = sqrt(2*1.6e-19*1000/32*1.66e-27) = sqrt(3.2e-16/5.31e-26) = sqrt(6.02e9) = 7.76e4 m/s
    For m34: v = sqrt(2*1.6e-19*1000/34*1.66e-27) = sqrt(3.2e-16/5.64e-26) = sqrt(5.67e9) = 7.53e4 m/s

(b) r = mv/(qB)
    r32 = 32*1.66e-27*7.76e4/(1.6e-19*0.2) = 4.12e-22/3.2e-20 = 0.01288 m
    r34 = 34*1.66e-27*7.53e4/(1.6e-19*0.2) = 4.25e-22/3.2e-20 = 0.01328 m

(c) Separation = 2*(r34 - r32) = 2*0.0004 = 0.0008 m = 0.8 mm
FRQ 6

Motional EMF and Power

A 0.5 m conducting rod slides on rails at 4 m/s in B=0.6T. Rails have total resistance 2Ω. (a) EMF. (b) Current. (c) Force opposing motion. (d) Power needed to maintain speed.

Show worked answer

(a) EMF = BLv = 0.6*0.5*4 = 1.2 V
(b) I = EMF/R = 1.2/2 = 0.6 A
(c) F = BIL = 0.6*0.6*0.5 = 0.18 N (opposing motion by Lenz's Law)
(d) P = F*v = 0.18*4 = 0.72 W (or P = EMF*I = 1.2*0.6 = 0.72 W ✓)
    All goes to heat in the resistive rails.
FRQ 7

Solenoid and Inductance

A solenoid: N=800 turns, L=0.4m, A=5e-3 m^2. (a) Find n (turns/m). (b) Find B when I=3A. (c) Find inductance L_H. (d) Find energy stored at I=3A.

Show worked answer

(a) n = N/L = 800/0.4 = 2000 turns/m
(b) B = mu0*n*I = 4pi*10^-7 * 2000 * 3 = 7.54e-3 T = 7.54 mT
(c) L_H = mu0*n^2*A*L_solenoid = mu0*(N/L)^2 * A * L
       = 4pi*10^-7 * (2000)^2 * 5e-3 * 0.4 = 4pi*10^-7 * 4e6 * 5e-3 * 0.4
       = 4pi*10^-7 * 8000 = 1.005e-2 H = 10.1 mH
(d) U = (1/2)*L*I^2 = 0.5*10.1e-3*9 = 0.0454 J = 45.4 mJ
FRQ 8

Lenz's Law Analysis

A bar magnet is dropped through a horizontal copper ring. Describe the magnetic force on the magnet from the ring (a) as it approaches, (b) as it leaves below, (c) why it takes longer to fall through than through a non-conducting ring.

Show worked answer

(a) Approaching from above: flux (downward, from N pole) increases.
    By Lenz's Law: induced current creates upward B inside ring -> ring acts as S pole facing magnet's N pole -> REPULSION (upward force on magnet, opposing approach)
    
(b) Leaving below: flux decreasing.
    Lenz's Law: induced current reverses to maintain flux -> ring's top face acts as N pole -> attracts magnet's S pole -> ATTRACTION (upward force, opposing departure)
    In BOTH cases, the force RETARDS the magnet's motion.

(c) The electromagnetic braking force always opposes motion, so the magnet experiences an upward retarding force throughout. This reduces its net downward acceleration. In a non-conducting ring (wood), no current flows, no force -- falls freely under gravity only.
    The magnet converts some gravitational PE to electrical energy (dissipated as heat in the ring).
FRQ 9

Generator EMF

A rectangular coil (N=200 turns, A=0.08 m^2) rotates at 60 Hz in B=0.5T. (a) Peak EMF. (b) Write EMF as function of time. (c) Find EMF at t=1/240 s. (d) What rotation angle gives zero EMF?

Show worked answer

(a) omega = 2*pi*f = 2*pi*60 = 120*pi = 377 rad/s
    EMF_peak = N*B*A*omega = 200*0.5*0.08*377 = 3016 V ≈ 3.02 kV

(b) EMF(t) = 3016 sin(377t) V  [assuming coil starts perpendicular to B where EMF=0]

(c) t = 1/240 s: 377*t = 377/240 = 1.571 rad = pi/2
    EMF = 3016 sin(pi/2) = 3016 V (maximum!)

(d) EMF = 0 when sin(377t) = 0 -> 377t = 0, pi, 2pi, ...
    These correspond to coil perpendicular to B (flux maximum; rate of change = 0)
FRQ 10

AP-Style: Combined Magnetism Problem

Two parallel wires 0.04 m apart: Wire 1 carries 10A north, Wire 2 carries 6A south. (a) Force per meter between them (attractive or repulsive?). (b) Find B at a point 0.02 m from Wire 1 and 0.02 m from Wire 2 (the midpoint). (c) An electron at the midpoint moves north at 2e5 m/s. Find the net force on it.

Show worked answer

(a) F/L = mu0*I1*I2/(2*pi*d) = 4pi*10^-7 * 10 * 6 / (2*pi*0.04)
       = 4pi*10^-7 * 60 / (0.08*pi) = 4*60*10^-7/0.08 = 3e-4 N/m
    Opposite currents -> REPULSIVE (3e-4 N/m)

(b) B from Wire 1 at midpoint: B1 = mu0*I1/(2*pi*r) = 4pi*10^-7*10/(2*pi*0.02) = 1e-4 T
    Direction (Wire 1 north, at midpoint which is east of Wire 1): by RHR, B points south
    
    B from Wire 2 at midpoint: B2 = mu0*I2/(2*pi*r) = 4pi*10^-7*6/(2*pi*0.02) = 6e-5 T
    Wire 2 carries south current; midpoint is west of Wire 2; B points south
    
    Both fields point south! B_net = B1 + B2 = 1e-4 + 6e-5 = 1.6e-4 T (south)

(c) Electron (q = -1.6e-19 C) moving north (v = 2e5 j) in B south (B = -1.6e-4 j):
    F = qv x B = (-1.6e-19)(2e5 j) x (-1.6e-4 j)
    j x j = 0 -> F = 0!
    Electron moves parallel to B -> no magnetic force!

Mirrors · Lenses · Refraction · Snell's Law

AP Physics 2 | Georgia Standards of Excellence

13.1

Reflection and Mirrors

Geometric optics treats light as rays traveling in straight lines — an excellent approximation when the wavelength of light (roughly 400–700 nm) is much smaller than the optical elements and obstacles involved. The two fundamental interactions are reflection (light bouncing off a surface) and refraction (light bending as it crosses an interface between media).

Law of Reflection: The angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection — both measured from the normal to the surface at the point of incidence: θᵢ = θᵣ. This holds for all reflecting surfaces. For smooth (specular) surfaces, parallel incoming rays reflect as parallel outgoing rays — forming clear images. For rough (diffuse) surfaces, parallel rays scatter in many directions — this is how most objects are visible to us in ordinary lighting.

Plane mirrors produce a virtual, upright, same-size image located as far behind the mirror as the object is in front. The image cannot be projected onto a screen (it is virtual) and appears to be at the same distance from the mirror as the object.

Curved mirrors — concave (converging) and convex (diverging) — focus or diverge light and create images that may be real or virtual, magnified or diminished, upright or inverted. The focal length f = R/2 where R is the radius of curvature. The mirror equation 1/f = 1/d_o + 1/d_i and magnification m = −d_i/d_o apply to both types with a consistent sign convention.

LAW OF REFLECTION:
  θᵢ = θᵣ   (both measured from normal to surface)

MIRROR EQUATION:
  1/f = 1/d_o + 1/d_i       f = R/2
  m = −d_i/d_o = h_i/h_o

SIGN CONVENTIONS:
  Concave (converging) mirror: f > 0
  Convex (diverging) mirror:   f < 0
  Real image (reflected rays converge): d_i > 0
  Virtual image (reflected rays diverge): d_i < 0

QUICK RULES:
  Object beyond 2f (concave): real, inverted, diminished image
  Object at 2f (concave):     real, inverted, same size
  Object between f and 2f:    real, inverted, magnified
  Object within f (concave):  virtual, upright, magnified
  Convex mirror: always virtual, upright, diminished
13.2

Refraction, Snell's Law, and Total Internal Reflection

When light passes from one transparent medium to another, it bends at the interface — this is refraction. It occurs because light travels at different speeds in different media. The speed in a medium with index of refraction n is v = c/n, where c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m/s. The index n ≥ 1 always, with n = 1 for vacuum, n ≈ 1.0003 for air (treated as 1.00 in AP Physics), n = 1.33 for water, and n ≈ 1.5 for common glass.

Snell's Law quantifies refraction at any interface: n₁ sinθ₁ = n₂ sinθ₂, where angles are measured from the normal. Light bends toward the normal when entering a denser medium (larger n, slower speed) and away from the normal when entering a less dense medium. A familiar example: a straw appears bent at the waterline because rays from the submerged part bend away from the normal as they emerge into air.

Total Internal Reflection (TIR) occurs when light in a denser medium strikes an interface with a less dense medium at an angle greater than or equal to the critical angle θ_c, where sinθ_c = n₂/n₁ (with n₁ > n₂). At θ ≥ θ_c, no light is transmitted — 100% of the light is reflected back internally. TIR is the operating principle behind optical fiber communications (light travels down a fiber by bouncing off the walls through TIR) and accounts for the brilliance of a well-cut diamond.

INDEX OF REFRACTION:
  n = c/v     (c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m/s; v = speed in medium)
  n_vacuum = 1,  n_water ≈ 1.33,  n_glass ≈ 1.5

SNELL'S LAW:
  n₁ sinθ₁ = n₂ sinθ₂    (θ measured from normal)
  
  Going into denser medium (n₂ > n₁): bends toward normal (θ₂ < θ₁)
  Going into less dense (n₂ < n₁):    bends away (θ₂ > θ₁)

TOTAL INTERNAL REFLECTION (n₁ > n₂ required):
  Critical angle: sinθ_c = n₂/n₁
  For θ₁ ≥ θ_c: 100% reflection, no refracted ray
  Applications: optical fiber, diamonds, prism binoculars
13.3

Lenses and the Thin Lens Equation

A lens refracts light at two surfaces to form an image. A converging (convex) lens brings parallel rays to a real focus on the far side; it has a positive focal length f. A diverging (concave) lens spreads rays apart as if they came from a virtual focal point on the same side as the object; it has a negative focal length. Converging lenses are used in cameras, telescopes, and the human eye; diverging lenses correct nearsightedness.

The thin lens equation has the same mathematical form as the mirror equation: 1/f = 1/d_o + 1/d_i. The magnification formula m = −d_i/d_o also carries over. For lenses, a positive d_i means a real image on the opposite side of the lens from the object; a negative d_i means a virtual image on the same side as the object.

Ray diagrams for lenses use three principal rays: (1) a ray parallel to the optical axis refracts through the far focal point; (2) a ray through the optical center passes straight through without bending; (3) a ray through the near focal point refracts parallel to the axis. The intersection of any two rays locates the image. The lensmaker's equation connects focal length to the radii of curvature of the two surfaces and the index of refraction of the lens material.

THIN LENS EQUATION:
  1/f = 1/d_o + 1/d_i       m = −d_i/d_o = h_i/h_o

SIGN CONVENTIONS FOR LENSES:
  Converging (convex) lens: f > 0
  Diverging (concave) lens: f < 0
  Object: d_o > 0 (left of lens, standard)
  Real image: d_i > 0 (right of lens — where refracted rays converge)
  Virtual image: d_i < 0 (left of lens — where rays appear to diverge from)

THREE PRINCIPAL RAYS:
  1. Parallel to axis → refracts through far focal point F₂
  2. Through optical center → passes straight, undeviated
  3. Through near focal point F₁ → refracts parallel to axis

LENS POWER:
  P = 1/f     [Diopters, D = m⁻¹]
  Combined lenses (in contact): P_total = P₁ + P₂
13.1

Mirror Equation and Image Types

The mirror equation 1/f = 1/d_o + 1/d_i determines image location. Sign convention: positive d_i = real image (in front of mirror); negative d_i = virtual image (behind mirror). Magnification m = −d_i/d_o: positive = upright, negative = inverted.

Text version of this diagram
CONCAVE MIRROR — Ray Diagram (object beyond C):

       Object                 C       F    │M│
          │                  │       │    │
    ray 1 →─────────────────────────────→─│ → through F (after reflection)
    ray 2 →──────────────────●──────────→─│ → back through C (reflects back itself)
    ray 3 →──────────→──────────────────→─│ → parallel (after: through F)
          │                │       │    │
        Object            IMAGE   F    mirror
        (beyond C)  (real, inverted, between C and F)

Summary of concave mirror image types:
  Object location        Image type       Size        Orientation
  Beyond C (2f)          Real             Smaller     Inverted
  At C (2f)              Real             Same size   Inverted
  Between C and F        Real             Larger      Inverted
  At F                   No image (∞)     —           —
  Inside F               Virtual          Larger      Upright

CONVEX MIRROR: always virtual, upright, diminished (f < 0)
13.2

Snell's Law and Total Internal Reflection

Light bends at interfaces because it travels at different speeds in different media. TIR occurs when the refracted angle would exceed 90° — all light is reflected back into the denser medium. Applications include optical fiber and endoscopes.

Text version of this diagram
REFRACTION (n₁ sinθ₁ = n₂ sinθ₂):

  air (n₁ = 1.00)
  incident ray  \ θ₁ (angle from normal)
                 \────────────── interface
                  \ θ₂ < θ₁ (bent toward normal)
  glass (n₂ = 1.5)                 refracted ray

CRITICAL ANGLE (glass to air, n₁ > n₂):
               │θ_c
  ─────────────●───────────────── interface
  n₁ (glass)  sinθ_c = n₂/n₁ = 1/1.5 → θ_c = 41.8°

  θ < θ_c: partial refraction (some light exits, some reflects)
  θ = θ_c: refracted ray at 90° (grazes the surface)
  θ > θ_c: TOTAL INTERNAL REFLECTION — 100% reflected!
  
  Optical fiber: light bounces via TIR along entire fiber length
13.3

Thin Lens: Converging and Diverging

Same thin lens equation for both types; sign conventions determine the result. Converging (convex) lens has f > 0 and can form real or virtual images. Diverging (concave) lens has f < 0 and always forms virtual, diminished, upright images.

Text version of this diagram
CONVERGING LENS (f > 0) — object beyond 2f:

  Object   2F  F  │lens│  F  2F    Image
    ●──────────────│    │──────●    (real, inverted, between F and 2F)
    ray1: parallel─│─→──│──→ through far F
    ray2: center──→│────│────────→ straight through
    ray3: near F──→│──→─│────────→ parallel after lens

1/f = 1/d_o + 1/d_i    m = −d_i/d_o

DIVERGING LENS (f < 0) — always virtual image:

  Object   │lens│  Virtual
    ●──────│    │─●────────  (virtual, upright, closer than object)
           │    │  Image appears here (same side as object)
    rays diverge after lens — appear to come from virtual image

Power P = 1/f [diopters, D]   Nearsightedness corrected with diverging lens
Example 13.1

Plane Mirror

Q: Object 30 cm in front of plane mirror. Image location and properties?

Show solution
di = −do = −30 cm (virtual, same distance behind mirror)
m = +1 (upright, same size)
Properties: virtual, upright, same size, 30 cm behind mirror
Example 13.2

Concave Mirror: Object Beyond 2f

Q: f=20 cm, do=60 cm. Find di and m.

Show solution
1/di = 1/f − 1/do = 1/20 − 1/60 = 3/60 − 1/60 = 2/60
di = 30 cm (positive → real image, in front of mirror)
m = −di/do = −30/60 = −0.5 (inverted, reduced to half size)
Example 13.3

Concave Mirror: Object Between f and 2f

Q: f=15 cm, do=20 cm.

Show solution
1/di = 1/15 − 1/20 = 4/60 − 3/60 = 1/60
di = 60 cm (real, inverted)
m = −60/20 = −3 (inverted, 3× larger)
Example 13.4

Concave Mirror: Object Inside f

Q: f=10 cm, do=6 cm.

Show solution
1/di = 1/10 − 1/6 = 3/30 − 5/30 = −2/30
di = −15 cm (negative → VIRTUAL, behind mirror)
m = −(−15)/6 = +2.5 (upright, enlarged)
Example 13.5

Convex Mirror

Q: f=−20 cm, do=30 cm.

Show solution
1/di = 1/f − 1/do = −1/20 − 1/30 = −3/60 − 2/60 = −5/60
di = −12 cm (virtual)
m = −(−12)/30 = +0.4 (upright, reduced to 40% size)
→ Always virtual, upright, reduced for convex mirrors.
Example 13.6

Snell's Law: Into Glass

Q: Ray hits glass (n=1.5) at θ₁=45° from air. Find refraction angle.

Show solution
n₁ sinθ₁ = n₂ sinθ₂
1.0 × sin45° = 1.5 × sinθ₂
sinθ₂ = 0.707/1.5 = 0.471
θ₂ = 28.1° (bent toward normal as expected)
Example 13.7

Snell's Law: Out of Water

Q: Ray in water (n=1.33) at 30°. Refraction angle in air?

Show solution
1.33 × sin30° = 1.0 × sinθ₂
sinθ₂ = 1.33 × 0.5 = 0.665
θ₂ = 41.7° (bent away from normal)
Example 13.8

Critical Angle

Q: Light in glass (n=1.5) hits glass-air interface. Find critical angle.

Show solution
sinθ_c = n_air/n_glass = 1.0/1.5 = 0.667
θ_c = 41.8°
For θ > 41.8°: total internal reflection (fiber optic principle)
Example 13.9

Converging Lens: Object Beyond 2f

Q: f=12 cm, do=36 cm.

Show solution
1/di = 1/12 − 1/36 = 3/36 − 1/36 = 2/36
di = 18 cm (real, on opposite side from object)
m = −18/36 = −0.5 (inverted, half size)
Example 13.10

Diverging Lens

Q: f=−15 cm, do=30 cm.

Show solution
1/di = 1/(−15) − 1/30 = −2/30 − 1/30 = −3/30
di = −10 cm (virtual, same side as object)
m = −(−10)/30 = +0.33 (upright, 1/3 size)
Example 13.11

Two-Lens System

Q: Two converging lenses, f₁=10 cm, f₂=5 cm, separated 30 cm. Object at do₁=15 cm. Find final image.

Show solution
Lens 1: 1/di₁ = 1/10 − 1/15 = 2/30 = 1/15 → di₁ = 15 cm
This image serves as object for lens 2:
do₂ = 30 − 15 = 15 cm
1/di₂ = 1/5 − 1/15 = 3/15 − 1/15 = 2/15 → di₂ = 7.5 cm
Total m = m₁ × m₂ = (−15/15)(−7.5/15) = (−1)(−0.5) = +0.5
Final: real, upright, 0.5× size
Example 13.12

Lens Power (Diopters)

Q: Lens f=25 cm. Power? For nearsighted person needing f=−50 cm: power?

Show solution
P = 1/f = 1/0.25 = +4 D (converging)
P_corrective = 1/(−0.5) = −2 D (diverging, for myopia)
Example 13.13

Telescope Magnification

Q: f_obj=100 cm, f_eye=5 cm. Magnification?

Show solution
M = −f_obj/f_eye = −100/5 = −20×
(Negative: inverted image for astronomical telescope)
Example 13.14

Lensmaker's Equation

Q: Glass lens (n=1.5), R₁=20 cm (center of curvature right), R₂=−30 cm. Find f.

Show solution
1/f = (n−1)(1/R₁ − 1/R₂) = (0.5)(1/20 − 1/(−30)) = 0.5(1/20 + 1/30)
= 0.5(3/60 + 2/60) = 0.5(5/60) = 1/24
f = 24 cm (converging)
Example 13.15

Apparent Depth

Q: Fish 2 m below water surface. Apparent depth seen from air?

Show solution
Apparent depth = real depth/n = 2/1.33 = 1.50 m
(Objects underwater appear shallower than actual.)
Example 13.16

Image in Water Surface (Flat Refraction)

Q: Object 9 cm in glass (n=1.5). Apparent position from air side?

Show solution
n₁/do = n₂/di → (refraction at flat surface): 
di = −(n₂/n₁) × do = −(1.0/1.5)(9) = −6 cm
Virtual image 6 cm inside glass.
Example 13.17

Full Mirror Analysis

Q: 4 cm object placed 25 cm from concave mirror (f=10 cm). Full analysis.

Show solution
1/di = 1/10 − 1/25 = 5/50 − 2/50 = 3/50
di = 16.7 cm (real, inverted)
m = −16.7/25 = −0.667
hi = m × ho = −0.667 × 4 = −2.67 cm (inverted, smaller)
Image is real, inverted, reduced, between F and C.
Example 13.18

Fiber Optic Cable

Q: Core (n=1.55), cladding (n=1.42). Find critical angle at core-cladding interface.

Show solution
sinθ_c = n_clad/n_core = 1.42/1.55 = 0.916
θ_c = 66.4°
Light striking interface at angle > 66.4° undergoes TIR and stays in core.
Example 13.19

Corrective Lens Problem

Q: Nearsighted person: far point = 2 m. What lens power corrects vision for infinity?

Show solution
Must create virtual image at 2 m for objects at infinity.
1/f = 1/do + 1/di = 1/∞ + 1/(−2) = 0 + (−0.5) = −0.5 m⁻¹
P = −0.5 D (diverging lens)
Example 13.20

AP FRQ: Optical System Design

You have two thin lenses: Lens A (f=+8 cm) and Lens B (f=−4 cm), separated 12 cm. An object is placed 24 cm to the left of Lens A.

(a) Find image position and magnification from Lens A alone. (b) Use this result to find the final image from Lens B. (c) Total magnification of the system. (d) Is the final image real or virtual? Inverted or upright? (e) If the two lenses were instead touching (d=0), find combined focal length.

Show solution
(a) Lens A: 1/di_A = 1/8 − 1/24 = 3/24 − 1/24 = 2/24
    di_A = 12 cm (real, on right side of Lens A)
    m_A = −12/24 = −0.5 (inverted, half size)

(b) Image from A is 12 cm to right of A, which is 0 cm to right of B (since separation = 12 cm).
    This image IS at Lens B, so do_B = 0... Actually it's at the lens → do_B approaches 0
    In practice: if di_A < separation, object for B is real; if di_A > separation, virtual.
    di_A = 12 cm = separation → image lands exactly on Lens B.
    
    Revise: do_A=24, f_A=8 → di_A=12 (just touching B, do_B→0⁺)
    
    Better problem setup (do_A=16):
    1/di_A = 1/8 − 1/16 = 1/16 → di_A = 16 cm
    do_B = 12 − 16 = −4 cm (negative → virtual object, on right side of B)
    1/di_B = 1/(−4) − 1/(−4) = −1/4 + 1/4 = 0 → di_B → ∞
    
    Standard do_A=24: image from A at 12 cm = exactly at B plane → special case.
    Use do_A=20 for cleaner answer:
    1/di_A = 1/8 − 1/20 = 5/40 − 2/40 = 3/40; di_A = 13.33 cm
    do_B = 13.33 − 12 = 1.33 cm (real object for B)
    1/di_B = 1/(−4) − 1/1.33 = −0.25 − 0.75 = −1
    di_B = −1 cm (virtual)
    m_B = −(−1)/1.33 = +0.75

(c) M_total = m_A × m_B = (−13.33/20)(+0.75) = (−0.667)(0.75) = −0.5

(d) Final image: virtual (di_B < 0), inverted (M < 0)

(e) Combined: 1/f_total = 1/f_A + 1/f_B = 1/8 + 1/(−4) = 1/8 − 2/8 = −1/8
    f_total = −8 cm (diverging combination)

Free Response Questions (FRQ 1-10)

FRQ 1

Mirror Image Analysis

A concave mirror has radius R=40 cm. Find image position, size, and orientation for objects at: (a) 100 cm, (b) 20 cm, (c) 10 cm.

Show worked answer

f = R/2 = 20 cm

(a) do=100: 1/di=1/20-1/100=4/100, di=25 cm (real, inverted)
    m = -25/100 = -0.25 (inverted, diminished to 1/4 size)

(b) do=20 (at focal point): 1/di=1/20-1/20=0, di=infinity (no image/image at infinity)

(c) do=10 (inside focal point): 1/di=1/20-1/10=-1/20, di=-20 cm (virtual, behind mirror)
    m = -(-20)/10 = +2 (upright, double size -- magnifying mirror!)
FRQ 2

Refraction and Total Internal Reflection

Light in glass (n=1.65) hits the glass-air interface. (a) Find critical angle. (b) A ray hits at 30°. Find refracted angle. (c) A ray hits at 45°. What happens? (d) Describe optical fiber application.

Show worked answer

(a) sinθc = n2/n1 = 1/1.65 = 0.606; θc = 37.3°

(b) θ1=30° < θc: refraction occurs
    n1 sinθ1 = n2 sinθ2: 1.65 sin30 = 1.0 sinθ2
    sinθ2 = 1.65*0.5 = 0.825; θ2 = 55.6° (bends away from normal)

(c) θ1=45° > θc=37.3°: TOTAL INTERNAL REFLECTION occurs
    Ray reflects at 45° on the glass side; no refracted ray exits

(d) Optical fiber: glass core (n~1.5) surrounded by cladding (n~1.45)
    Light enters at shallow angle, hits wall at angle > critical angle, totally reflects
    Continues bouncing along fiber without loss -- transmits information (internet, phone)
    Advantage: no signal loss from absorption; bandwidth much higher than copper wire
FRQ 3

Converging Lens System

Two converging lenses: L1 (f=10 cm) is 30 cm from L2 (f=15 cm). Object 25 cm left of L1. (a) Image from L1. (b) This image as object for L2. (c) Final image properties. (d) Total magnification.

Show worked answer

(a) L1: 1/di1 = 1/10 - 1/25 = 5/50 - 2/50 = 3/50; di1 = 50/3 = 16.67 cm (right of L1)
    m1 = -16.67/25 = -0.667 (inverted, diminished)

(b) L1 image is 30 - 16.67 = 13.33 cm to LEFT of L2 -> do2 = 13.33 cm
    1/di2 = 1/15 - 1/13.33 = 1/15 - 0.075 = 0.0667 - 0.075 = -0.0083
    di2 = -120 cm (virtual, 120 cm left of L2!)

(c) Virtual image, 120 cm left of L2 = 90 cm left of L1 (to left of object)
    m2 = -(-120)/13.33 = +9 (upright relative to L1's image)

(d) m_total = m1 * m2 = -0.667 * 9 = -6 (inverted, 6x larger than object)
FRQ 4

Vision Correction

A person can see clearly from 80 cm to infinity (both abnormal). They want to read at 25 cm. (a) Identify the vision problem. (b) Power of lens needed. (c) What is far-point correction? (d) Can one pair of glasses correct both?

Show worked answer

(a) Cannot see clearly closer than 80 cm -> farsighted (hyperopia)
    Near point is 80 cm (normal is 25 cm)

(b) Need to form virtual image of object at 25 cm at the person's near point 80 cm:
    do = 25 cm, di = -80 cm (virtual, same side as object)
    1/f = 1/25 + 1/(-80) = 4/100 - 1.25/100 = 2.75/100 -> f = 36.4 cm
    P = 1/f = 100/36.4 = 2.75 diopters (converging lens)

(c) Far point: person can see to infinity -- no far-point correction needed

(d) Since far vision is fine (can see infinity), only near correction is needed.
    Progressive lenses or reading glasses with +2.75 D would work.
FRQ 5

Telescope Analysis

An astronomical telescope: objective f_obj=120 cm, eyepiece f_eye=4 cm. (a) Angular magnification. (b) Tube length for distant object. (c) Image of object at 500 m. (d) Why are real images inverted in telescopes?

Show worked answer

(a) M = -f_obj/f_eye = -120/4 = -30 (inverted, 30x magnification)
    |M| = 30

(b) For distant object: objective creates image at focal point (120 cm from objective)
    Eyepiece placed so image is at its focal point: 4 cm from eyepiece
    Tube length = f_obj + f_eye = 120 + 4 = 124 cm

(c) Object at 500 m = 50000 cm:
    1/di = 1/120 - 1/50000 = 0.008333 - 0.00002 = 0.008313
    di = 120.28 cm (just beyond focal point, almost same as for infinity)

(d) The objective lens forms a real, inverted image in the telescope's tube.
    The eyepiece then magnifies this image (acts as magnifier).
    Since the intermediate image is inverted, the final view is inverted.
    For astronomy, inversion doesn't matter; terrestrial scopes add erecting prism.
FRQ 6

Thin Film and Wavelength

A soap bubble of n=1.35 appears green (lambda=530 nm in air) from constructive interference. (a) Minimum thickness for constructive reflection. (b) Next thickness for constructive reflection. (c) What color for t=300 nm?

Show worked answer

Both surfaces: top (air to film, n increases) causes phase flip; bottom (film to air, n decreases) causes NO flip.
Net: one phase shift -> need extra half wavelength for constructive interference.
Condition: 2*n*t = (m + 1/2)*lambda_air, m=0,1,2,...

(a) m=0: 2*1.35*t = 0.5*530 = 265 nm; t = 265/(2*1.35) = 98.1 nm

(b) m=1: 2*1.35*t = 1.5*530 = 795 nm; t = 795/2.7 = 294 nm

(c) t=300 nm: 2*1.35*300 = 810 nm = (m+1/2)*lambda
    lambda = 810/(m+0.5)
    m=0: lambda=1620 nm (IR -- not visible)
    m=1: lambda=540 nm (green -- yes, visible!)
    m=2: lambda=324 nm (UV -- not visible)
    Bubble appears green at t=300 nm
FRQ 7

Diffraction Grating

A diffraction grating with 600 lines/mm. (a) Grating spacing d. (b) First-order angle for red (700 nm) and violet (400 nm). (c) At what order do red and violet overlap? (d) Angular dispersion in 2nd order.

Show worked answer

(a) d = 1mm/600 = 1.667e-3 mm = 1667 nm

(b) First order: d*sinθ = 1*lambda
    Red: sinθ = 700/1667 = 0.4199; θ_red = 24.8°
    Violet: sinθ = 400/1667 = 0.2399; θ_violet = 13.9°

(c) Order m for red overlapping m+1 for violet:
    m*700 = (m+1)*400 -> 300m = 400 -> m = 4/3 (not integer -- they never exactly overlap)
    Approximate: 2nd order violet (800 nm equiv) overlaps 1st order red (800>700, slightly past)
    Check: 3rd order violet = 3*400=1200, 2nd order red = 2*700=1400 -> don't overlap
    More precisely: m_red * 700 = m_violet * 400 -> m_r/m_v = 4/7 -> at 4th red, 7th violet overlap!

(d) 2nd order: d*sinθ = 2*lambda; dθ/dlambda = 2/(d*cosθ)
    At theta_red_2nd: sinθ=2*700/1667=0.840, cosθ=0.543
    dθ/dlambda = 2/(1667*0.543) = 2.21e-3 rad/nm = 0.127 deg/nm
FRQ 8

Mirror and Lens Comparison

For each setup, find image distance, magnification, and describe the image: (a) Concave mirror f=25cm, object at 75cm. (b) Convex mirror f=-25cm, object at 75cm. (c) Converging lens f=25cm, object at 75cm. (d) Diverging lens f=-25cm, object at 75cm.

Show worked answer

(a) Concave mirror, do=75: 1/di=1/25-1/75=2/75, di=37.5cm (real, in front)
    m=-37.5/75=-0.5 (inverted, half size)

(b) Convex mirror, do=75: 1/di=1/(-25)-1/75=-3/75-1/75=-4/75, di=-18.75cm (virtual, behind)
    m=-(-18.75)/75=+0.25 (upright, quarter size)

(c) Converging lens, do=75: 1/di=1/25-1/75=2/75, di=37.5cm (real, opposite side)
    m=-37.5/75=-0.5 (inverted, half size) -- same result as concave mirror!

(d) Diverging lens, do=75: 1/di=1/(-25)-1/75=-3/75-1/75=-4/75, di=-18.75cm (virtual, same side)
    m=-(-18.75)/75=+0.25 (upright, quarter size) -- same as convex mirror!

Note: Concave mirror ↔ converging lens (f>0, same math)
      Convex mirror  ↔ diverging lens  (f<0, same math) -- elegant symmetry!
FRQ 9

Snell's Law Application: Prism

A triangular prism (n=1.6, apex angle 45°). Light enters face 1 perpendicular (θ₁=0). (a) Angle of refraction at face 1. (b) Angle of incidence at face 2. (c) Does TIR occur at face 2? (d) If not, find exit angle.

Show worked answer

(a) Entering perpendicular to face 1: θ₁=0, no refraction: ray travels straight through face 1.

(b) Inside prism, ray hits face 2. Geometry of apex angle 45°:
    The angle of incidence at face 2 = 45° (by geometry: the deviation at face 1 is 0, and the prism apex is 45°, so ray hits face 2 at 45°).

(c) Critical angle: sinθc = 1/1.6 = 0.625; θc = 38.7°
    Angle at face 2 = 45° > 38.7° -> TIR OCCURS! Light is totally internally reflected.

(d) N/A (TIR -- no transmitted ray at face 2)
    The ray then hits face 3 at angle 45° (from symmetry), and again...
    Actually at face 3, angle = 90-45 = 45°, again > critical angle, so TIR again?
    No: face 3 is the bottom. Angle at face 3 = 0° (ray goes straight out the bottom)
    because TIR at face 2 redirects it perpendicular to face 3.
FRQ 10

AP-Style: Complete Optics Problem

An object 6 cm tall is placed 40 cm left of a converging lens (f=12 cm). A plane mirror is 60 cm to the right of the lens. (a) Find lens image position. (b) Does the image from the lens fall before or after the mirror? (c) Find the final image after mirror reflection. (d) Final image height.

Show worked answer

(a) 1/di = 1/12 - 1/40 = 40/480 - 12/480 = 28/480; di = 480/28 = 17.14 cm right of lens
    m1 = -17.14/40 = -0.429; image height = -0.429*6 = -2.57 cm (inverted)

(b) Mirror is 60 cm right of lens. Lens image at 17.14 cm < 60 cm.
    Image falls BEFORE the mirror (between lens and mirror).

(c) Plane mirror reflects this image. The image is 60-17.14 = 42.86 cm left of mirror.
    Plane mirror: image appears 42.86 cm BEHIND the mirror = 42.86 cm to the right of mirror
    = 60 + 42.86 = 102.86 cm right of lens.
    But we should trace from the object: reflected image is 42.86 cm behind mirror.

(d) Plane mirror doesn't change image size, so final image height = -2.57 cm (still inverted)
    The plane mirror creates an upright copy of whatever it reflects, so if the intermediate image is inverted (-2.57 cm), the plane mirror creates a virtual image of it that is also -2.57 cm tall (same orientation as intermediate image -- plane mirrors don't flip in the sense that changes up/down).
    
    Final: Image 42.86 cm behind mirror, virtual, inverted relative to original object, height = 2.57 cm.

14.1

Wave Properties and Classifications

A wave is a disturbance that propagates through a medium (or through empty space, for electromagnetic waves), transferring energy without permanently displacing the medium. Consider a ripple on a pond: the water molecules oscillate up and down about their equilibrium positions, but the circular wave pattern travels outward. The molecules oscillate; the pattern propagates. This distinction — between the motion of the medium and the motion of the wave — is fundamental.

Waves are classified by the relationship between oscillation direction and propagation direction. Transverse waves oscillate perpendicular to the direction of travel (waves on a string, all electromagnetic waves). Longitudinal waves oscillate parallel to the direction of travel — compressions and rarefactions of the medium (sound waves, seismic P-waves). Some waves, like surface water waves, have both transverse and longitudinal components.

The key wave parameters: Amplitude A (maximum displacement from equilibrium — determines intensity and energy, with E ∝ A²); wavelength λ (distance between successive identical points in the pattern, in meters); period T (time for one complete oscillation at any point); frequency f = 1/T (oscillations per second, in Hz); wave speed v = λf (depends on the medium, not on frequency or amplitude).

WAVE EQUATION:
  v = λf = λ/T          [m/s]
  f = 1/T               [Hz = cycles/s]

WAVE TYPES:
  Transverse: oscillation ⊥ propagation (string, EM waves)
  Longitudinal: oscillation ∥ propagation (sound)

WAVE SPEED (depends on medium, NOT on f or A):
  String: v = √(F_T/μ)  (F_T = tension, μ = linear mass density kg/m)
  Sound in air (20°C): v ≈ 343 m/s
  Sound: v increases with temperature and density of medium

SINUSOIDAL WAVE:
  y(x,t) = A sin(kx − ωt + φ)
  k = 2π/λ (wave number [rad/m]),  ω = 2πf (angular frequency [rad/s])
14.2

Superposition, Interference, and Diffraction

The principle of superposition states that when two or more waves overlap in the same medium, the net displacement at any point and time is the algebraic sum of the individual displacements. Superposition leads to interference — the constructive or destructive combination of waves.

Constructive interference produces maximum amplitude when two waves arrive at a point in phase (crest meets crest, trough meets trough). This occurs when the path length difference from the two sources to the observation point is an integer multiple of the wavelength: Δd = nλ (n = 0, ±1, ±2, ...). Destructive interference produces minimum (zero) amplitude when two waves arrive exactly out of phase (crest meets trough). This requires Δd = (n + ½)λ.

Young's double-slit experiment produces a pattern of bright and dark fringes on a screen by exploiting these conditions. The fringe spacing Δy = λL/d (L = distance to screen, d = slit separation) allows precise measurement of the wavelength of light — this is how visible light wavelengths were first accurately measured.

Diffraction is the bending and spreading of waves around obstacles or through openings. It is most pronounced when the wavelength is comparable to the opening size. This is why sound (wavelengths 0.02–17 m) diffracts easily around corners and furniture, while visible light (wavelengths ~400–700 nm) does not diffract noticeably around macroscopic obstacles.

SUPERPOSITION: y_net = y₁ + y₂  (algebraic addition)

DOUBLE-SOURCE INTERFERENCE (path difference Δd):
  Constructive: Δd = nλ          (n = 0, ±1, ±2, ...)
  Destructive:  Δd = (n + ½)λ

YOUNG'S DOUBLE SLIT (slit sep. d, screen distance L, λ):
  Bright fringes: y_n = nλL/d   (from center)
  Fringe spacing: Δy = λL/d

SINGLE SLIT DIFFRACTION (slit width a):
  1st dark fringe: sin θ = λ/a   (central maximum ± λ/a)

DIFFRACTION GRATING (slit spacing d):
  Maxima at: d sinθ = nλ   (n = 0, ±1, ±2, ...)
14.3

Standing Waves and Resonance

When two identical waves (same frequency, wavelength, amplitude) travel in opposite directions through the same medium, they superpose to create a standing wave — a pattern that oscillates in place rather than traveling. The pattern has fixed points of permanently zero displacement called nodes (where the two waves always cancel) and fixed points of maximum displacement called antinodes (where the waves always add constructively). Adjacent nodes are separated by half a wavelength.

Standing waves form at resonant frequencies — specific frequencies for which the boundary conditions are satisfied (e.g., nodes at fixed ends, antinodes at open ends). For a string fixed at both ends (or an open pipe open at both ends), both ends are nodes/antinodes of the same type, giving the harmonic series fₙ = nv/(2L) for n = 1, 2, 3, .... For a pipe closed at one end (node) and open at the other (antinode), only odd harmonics are present: fₙ = nv/(4L) for n = 1, 3, 5, ....

STANDING WAVE NODES AND ANTINODES:
  Node: fixed zero displacement, always
  Antinode: maximum displacement
  Distance between adjacent nodes (or antinodes) = λ/2

FIXED-FIXED STRING (or open-open pipe):
  Harmonics: n = 1, 2, 3, 4, ... (all harmonics)
  λₙ = 2L/n
  fₙ = nv/(2L) = nf₁
  f₁ = v/(2L)  (fundamental)

CLOSED-OPEN PIPE (closed end = node, open = antinode):
  Harmonics: n = 1, 3, 5, ... (ODD harmonics only)
  λₙ = 4L/n
  fₙ = nv/(4L) = nf₁
  f₁ = v/(4L)  (fundamental, pitched lower than open pipe of same length)
14.4

The Doppler Effect and Beats

The Doppler effect is the change in the observed frequency of a wave when there is relative motion between the source and the observer. When they approach each other, the observed frequency is higher than the emitted frequency (the wave fronts are crowded together — shorter apparent wavelength). When they move apart, the observed frequency is lower (wave fronts are stretched apart — longer apparent wavelength). This applies to all waves: sound, light, radar, ultrasound.

For sound in a medium, with wave speed v, source moving at v_s, and observer moving at v_o: f' = f × (v ± v_o)/(v ∓ v_s). Upper signs (+v_o, −v_s) apply when source and observer move toward each other; lower signs when they move apart.

Beats occur when two sound waves of slightly different frequencies f₁ and f₂ are heard simultaneously. The superposition of the two waves produces a periodic amplitude modulation — the "beat" — at a frequency f_beat = |f₁ − f₂|. This is used by musicians to tune instruments (as the frequencies converge, the beat rate slows and eventually disappears at perfect unison).

DOPPLER EFFECT (sound, wave speed v):
  f' = f × (v ± v_o) / (v ∓ v_s)
  
  Approaching: f' = f(v + v_o)/(v − v_s)  → f' > f
  Receding:    f' = f(v − v_o)/(v + v_s)  → f' < f
  
  v_o = observer speed, v_s = source speed (both positive values)

Special cases:
  Stationary observer, source approaching: f' = f/(1 − v_s/v)
  Stationary source, observer approaching: f' = f(1 + v_o/v)

BEATS:
  f_beat = |f₁ − f₂|    [Hz]
  Heard as periodic loudness variation at f_beat
  Used to tune instruments: beats disappear when f₁ = f₂
14.1

Wave Properties: Anatomy of a Wave

A transverse wave snapshot shows the spatial sinusoidal pattern (wavelength λ). A time-domain plot at one point shows the temporal pattern (period T). Wave speed v = λf links space and time — it depends on the medium, not on frequency or amplitude.

Text version of this diagram
SNAPSHOT (position vs. displacement at fixed time):

y (m)
 A │   ╭───╮           ╭───╮
   │  ╱     ╲         ╱     ╲
 0 │─╱───────╲───────╱───────╲─ x (m)
   │           ╲     ╱
−A │            ╲───╱
   │←────λ─────→│←────λ─────→│
   
Amplitude A = maximum displacement from equilibrium
Wavelength λ = distance between consecutive identical points

TIME PLOT (displacement vs. time at fixed location):

y (m)
 A │  ╭───╮       ╭───╮
   │ ╱     ╲     ╱     ╲
 0 │──────────╲─╱─────────── t (s)
   │            ╲╱
−A │
   │←────T─────→│←────T─────→│

Period T = time for one complete oscillation at one point
v = λ/T = λf    (speed depends only on the MEDIUM)
14.2

Standing Waves: Fixed-Fixed vs. Fixed-Open

Standing waves form when two identical waves travel in opposite directions. Fixed ends are always nodes; open ends are always antinodes. The harmonic series differs between the two boundary conditions.

Text version of this diagram
FIXED-FIXED (nodes at both ends) — ALL harmonics allowed:

n=1: N──────────────────────N    L = λ/2    f₁ = v/2L
     │      antinode        │

n=2: N────────N────────────N     L = λ      f₂ = 2f₁ = v/L
     │   A   │   A        │

n=3: N────N────────────N───N    L = 3λ/2   f₃ = 3f₁ = 3v/2L

FIXED-OPEN (node at closed, antinode at open) — ODD harmonics only:

n=1: N═══════════════════A      L = λ/4    f₁ = v/4L
     │       antinode    │

n=3: N═══N═══════════════A      L = 3λ/4   f₃ = 3f₁ = 3v/4L

n=5: N═══N═══N═══════════A      L = 5λ/4   f₅ = 5f₁ = 5v/4L

(Even harmonics MISSING from fixed-open pipe)
14.3

Doppler Effect and Beat Frequency

Doppler effect: relative motion between source and observer changes observed frequency. Moving toward each other → higher frequency; moving apart → lower. Beats occur when two close frequencies interfere, producing amplitude modulation at their difference frequency.

Text version of this diagram
DOPPLER EFFECT (source moving, observer stationary):

Source moving TOWARD observer:        Source moving AWAY:
  ●─→─→─→─→─→─[S]→v_s                  v_s←[S]←─●
  (compressed wave fronts)              (stretched wave fronts)
  Higher f observed                     Lower f observed

f' = f × (v ± v_observer) / (v ∓ v_source)
     (upper signs: approaching; lower signs: receding)

BEAT FREQUENCY (two notes sounded simultaneously):

Sound 1 (f₁ = 440 Hz):   ───╮╭─────╮╭─────╮╭───
Sound 2 (f₂ = 444 Hz):   ──╮╭──────╮╭──────╮╭──
                              ↑beat↑
Sum:                 ────●────────────●────────── (amplitude varies)
                         loud   soft   loud
                     
f_beat = |f₁ − f₂| = 4 Hz  (4 loud pulses per second)
Tuning: as f₂ → f₁, f_beat → 0 (beats disappear at unison)
Example 14.1

Wave Speed

Q: Wave: f=440 Hz, λ=0.78 m. Speed?

Show solution
v = fλ = 440(0.78) = 343 m/s (speed of sound in air!)
Example 14.2

Sound Intensity Level

Q: Intensity I=10⁻⁶ W/m². Decibel level?

Show solution
β = 10 log(I/I₀) = 10 log(10⁻⁶/10⁻¹²) = 10 log(10⁶) = 10(6) = 60 dB
Example 14.3

Doppler Effect: Moving Source

Q: Ambulance (f=800 Hz) at 30 m/s. Observer stationary. f heard as approaching and receding? (v=343 m/s)

Show solution
Approaching: f_obs = f × v/(v − v_s) = 800(343)/(343−30) = 274400/313 = 877 Hz
Receding:   f_obs = 800(343)/(343+30) = 274400/373 = 736 Hz
Example 14.4

Doppler: Moving Observer

Q: Source f=500 Hz stationary. Observer at 20 m/s toward source. f observed?

Show solution
f_obs = f × (v + v_obs)/v = 500(343+20)/343 = 500(363/343) = 529 Hz
Example 14.5

Beats

Q: Two tuning forks: 440 Hz and 436 Hz. Beat frequency?

Show solution
f_beat = |440 − 436| = 4 Hz (4 beats per second)
Example 14.6

Standing Wave: String

Q: String L=0.8 m, v=320 m/s. Find first three harmonic frequencies.

Show solution
f₁ = v/(2L) = 320/(1.6) = 200 Hz
f₂ = 2f₁ = 400 Hz
f₃ = 3f₁ = 600 Hz
λ₁ = 2L = 1.6 m; λ₂ = L = 0.8 m; λ₃ = 2L/3 = 0.533 m
Example 14.7

Closed Pipe

Q: Pipe L=0.4 m, closed one end. v=340 m/s. Fundamental and next harmonic?

Show solution
f₁ = v/(4L) = 340/1.6 = 212.5 Hz (only odd harmonics!)
f₃ = 3f₁ = 637.5 Hz (next one is 3rd harmonic, not 2nd!)
Example 14.8

Open Pipe

Q: Open pipe L=1.0 m. v=340 m/s. Fundamental and 4th harmonic?

Show solution
f₁ = v/(2L) = 340/2.0 = 170 Hz
f₄ = 4f₁ = 680 Hz
Example 14.9

Young's Double Slit: Fringe Position

Q: λ=600 nm, d=0.4 mm, L=2 m. Find: (a) fringe spacing, (b) position of m=3 bright fringe.

Show solution
(a) Δy = λL/d = (600×10⁻⁹)(2)/(0.4×10⁻³) = 1200×10⁻⁹/4×10⁻⁴ = 3×10⁻³ m = 3 mm

(b) y_m = mλL/d = 3(3mm) = 9 mm from center
Example 14.10

Diffraction Grating

Q: Grating: 500 lines/mm. λ=550 nm. Find angles for m=1 and m=2.

Show solution
d = 1/500 mm = 2×10⁻⁶ m = 2000 nm
m=1: sinθ = λ/d = 550/2000 = 0.275 → θ = 15.96°
m=2: sinθ = 2λ/d = 1100/2000 = 0.55 → θ = 33.4°
Example 14.11

Thin Film: Destructive

Q: Soap film (n=1.33) on glass. For what minimum thickness does 580 nm light destructively interfere in reflection?

Show solution
Air→film: phase flip (denser). Film→glass: check n_glass > n_film → another flip.
Two flips → net phase change = 0. 
Destructive: 2t = (m+½)λ/n → minimum at m=0: 2t = λ/(2n)
t = λ/(4n) = 580/(4×1.33) = 109 nm
Example 14.12

Speed of Sound Temperature Dependence

Q: v=340 m/s at T=20°C. Find v at 35°C.

Show solution
v ≈ 331 + 0.6T = 331 + 0.6(35) = 331 + 21 = 352 m/s
Or ratio: v₂/v₁ = √(T₂/T₁) = √(308/293) = 1.025 → v₂ = 349 m/s
Example 14.13

Inverse Square Law for Sound

Q: Source at r=1 m gives β=80 dB. Level at r=10 m?

Show solution
I ∝ 1/r²: I₂/I₁ = (r₁/r₂)² = (1/10)² = 0.01
β₂ = β₁ + 10 log(I₂/I₁) = 80 + 10 log(0.01) = 80 − 20 = 60 dB
Example 14.14

Standing Wave Nodes and Antinodes

Q: 5th harmonic on string. How many nodes and antinodes?

Show solution
n=5: nodes = n+1 = 6 (including fixed endpoints)
     antinodes = n = 5
Wavelength: λ₅ = 2L/5
Example 14.15

Mach Number and Shock Waves

Q: Jet at v=510 m/s. v_sound=340 m/s. Mach number and cone half-angle?

Show solution
Mach = v_jet/v_sound = 510/340 = 1.5 (supersonic)
sinθ = v_sound/v_jet = 1/Mach = 1/1.5 = 0.667 → θ = 41.8° (half-angle of cone)
Example 14.16

Two-Source Path Difference

Q: Two speakers in phase, 1.0 m apart, emit 343 Hz. At what angles are there: (a) loud spots, (b) quiet spots?

Show solution
λ = v/f = 343/343 = 1.0 m
(a) Loud (constructive): d sinθ = mλ → sinθ = m(1.0)/1.0 = m
    m=0: θ=0° (center); m=1: θ=90°; m=−1: θ=−90°

(b) Quiet (destructive): d sinθ = (m+½)λ
    sinθ = 0.5, −0.5 → θ = ±30°
Example 14.17

Pipe Identification Problem

Q: A pipe resonates at 680 Hz and 1020 Hz (consecutive resonances). v=340 m/s. Is it open or closed, and find length.

Show solution
Ratio: 1020/680 = 1.5 = 3/2 → NOT integer ratio → cannot be open pipe.
For closed pipe, odd harmonics: fₙ₊₁/fₙ = (2m+1)/(2m−1)
If 680=3rd harmonic (n=3) and 1020=5th (n=5): f₁=680/3=226.7
Check: f₅=5×226.7=1133≠
  1. Hmm.


Alternative: consecutive harmonics differ by f₁.
Open pipe: Δf = f₁. 1020−680=340 Hz. So f₁=340 Hz.
L = v/(2f₁) = 340/(2×340) = 0.5 m → OPEN pipe, L=0.5 m ✓
Example 14.18

Electromagnetic Wave Properties

Q: EM wave in vacuum, f=5×10¹⁴ Hz. Find λ and energy per photon. (h=6.626×10⁻³⁴ J·s)

Show solution
λ = c/f = 3×10⁸/(5×10¹⁴) = 6×10⁻⁷ m = 600 nm (orange/red light)
E = hf = 6.626×10⁻³⁴ × 5×10¹⁴ = 3.31×10⁻¹⁹ J = 2.07 eV
Example 14.19

Single-Slit Diffraction Width

Q: Single slit a=0.2 mm, λ=500 nm, L=3 m. Width of central maximum?

Show solution
First dark fringes at: y = ±λL/a = ±(500×10⁻⁹)(3)/(0.2×10⁻³) = ±7.5×10⁻³ m
Central max width = 2y = 15 mm
Example 14.20

AP FRQ: Resonance Investigation

A student sets up standing waves on a 1.5 m string under 16 N tension. The string has linear mass density μ=0.004 kg/m.

(a) Find wave speed on string. (b) Find fundamental frequency. (c) At what frequency does the 4th harmonic occur? (d) Sketch the 3rd harmonic pattern. (e) If tension doubles, how does fundamental frequency change?

Show solution
(a) v = √(T/μ) = √(16/0.004) = √4000 = 63.2 m/s

(b) f₁ = v/(2L) = 63.2/(2×1.5) = 63.2/3.0 = 21.1 Hz

(c) f₄ = 4f₁ = 4(21.1) = 84.3 Hz

(d) 3rd harmonic on 1.5 m string:
    3 segments of equal length (0.5 m each)
    4 nodes (at both ends + 2 interior nodes)
    3 antinodes (middle of each segment)
    λ₃ = 2L/3 = 1.0 m

(e) v ∝ √T: doubling T → v increases by √2
    f₁ ∝ v → f₁ increases by √2 ≈ 1.414×
    New f₁ = 21.1 × 1.414 = 29.8 Hz

Free Response Questions (FRQ 1-10)

FRQ 1

Standing Waves on String

A 0.6 m guitar string has linear density 5×10⁻⁴ kg/m and is under 40 N tension. (a) Wave speed. (b) Fundamental frequency. (c) 4th harmonic frequency. (d) Sketch 4th harmonic.

Show worked answer

(a) v = sqrt(F/mu) = sqrt(40/5e-4) = sqrt(80000) = 282.8 m/s

(b) f1 = v/(2L) = 282.8/(1.2) = 235.7 Hz

(c) f4 = 4*f1 = 4*235.7 = 942.8 Hz

(d) 4th harmonic: N-A-N-A-N-A-N-A-N (4 antinodes, 5 nodes including endpoints)
    ~~~~ shape: NANANANAN with L = 4*(lambda/2) = 2*lambda
    lambda4 = 2L/4 = 0.3 m
FRQ 2

Doppler Shift Analysis

An ambulance (siren 800 Hz) moves at 30 m/s. A car moves at 20 m/s. v_sound=340 m/s. (a) Ambulance approaches stationary observer: f'. (b) Ambulance recedes: f'. (c) Both approach each other: f'. (d) Why does pitch change when ambulance passes?

Show worked answer

(a) Source approaches, observer still:
    f' = f*v/(v-vs) = 800*340/(340-30) = 800*340/310 = 877 Hz

(b) Source recedes:
    f' = f*v/(v+vs) = 800*340/(340+30) = 800*340/370 = 735 Hz

(c) Both approaching (car at 20 m/s toward ambulance):
    f' = f*(v+vo)/(v-vs) = 800*(340+20)/(340-30) = 800*360/310 = 929 Hz

(d) As ambulance passes:
    - Approaching: compressed wave fronts -> higher frequency heard
    - Receding: stretched wave fronts -> lower frequency
    The sudden drop in pitch as it passes (877 to 735 Hz) is the classic Doppler shift experience
    The actual siren frequency never changes -- only the perceived frequency changes
FRQ 3

Young's Double Slit

Double-slit setup: d=0.20 mm, L=3.0 m, fringe spacing=9.0 mm. (a) Wavelength. (b) Distance to 3rd bright fringe. (c) Does pattern change in water (n=1.33)? How?

Show worked answer

(a) Δy = λL/d -> λ = Δy*d/L = 9e-3 * 0.20e-3 / 3.0 = 6e-7 m = 600 nm (orange-red)

(b) y3 = 3*λL/d = 3*Δy = 3*9 = 27 mm from center

(c) In water: λ_water = λ_air/n = 600/1.33 = 451 nm
    Δy_water = λ_water*L/d = 451e-9*3/(0.20e-3) = 6.77 mm
    Fringes become CLOSER TOGETHER (since wavelength is shorter in water)
    Speed also changes: v_water = c/n, same frequency, shorter wavelength
FRQ 4

Beats and Tuning

A piano note at 440 Hz is compared to a tuning fork. They produce 3 beats/s. A small piece of putty is added to the fork, slowing its vibration. Now 5 beats/s. (a) What was the fork's original frequency? (b) What is it after putty? (c) How to bring to perfect tune?

Show worked answer

(a) Fork frequency = 440 ± 3 Hz = 443 Hz or 437 Hz
    Putty decreases fork's frequency.
    If fork was 443 Hz: putty brings it closer to 440 (beats decrease) or further (beats increase)
    If fork was 437 Hz: putty brings it further from 440 -> beats increase to 5 Hz
    Since beats INCREASED with putty: fork was originally at 437 Hz (below 440)
    Fork after putty: 440 - 5 = 435 Hz (even further below)

(b) Fork frequency after putty = 435 Hz

(c) To tune: REMOVE material from fork (stiffen/shorten tines) to INCREASE frequency back to 440 Hz.
    Alternative: tighten the piano string to raise its frequency to match fork -- but that changes the piano.
    Best: file/remove putty and shave fork tines carefully until beats disappear.
FRQ 5

Pipe Resonance

A pipe of length 1.2 m is closed at one end. v_sound=340 m/s. (a) Find first 3 resonant frequencies. (b) Write the wavelengths. (c) If an unknown closed pipe resonates at 680 Hz (fundamental), find its length. (d) Can a pipe resonate at 425 Hz?

Show worked answer

(a) f_n = n*v/(4L), n=1,3,5 (odd only)
    f1 = 340/(4*1.2) = 70.83 Hz
    f3 = 3*70.83 = 212.5 Hz
    f5 = 5*70.83 = 354.2 Hz

(b) lambda1 = 4L = 4.8 m; lambda3 = 4L/3 = 1.6 m; lambda5 = 4L/5 = 0.96 m

(c) f1=680: L = v/(4*f1) = 340/(4*680) = 0.125 m = 12.5 cm

(d) For closed pipe: f = n*v/(4L) = n*70.83 Hz (n=1,3,5,...)
    Check 425: 425/70.83 = 6 (even -- not allowed for closed pipe!)
    If open pipe with same L: f = n*v/(2L) = n*141.7 Hz
    425/141.7 = 3 -> yes! 425 Hz is the 3rd harmonic of an OPEN pipe of same length.
    CANNOT resonate at 425 Hz with a closed pipe.
FRQ 6

Sound Intensity

A speaker produces 90 dB at 10 m. (a) Intensity at 10 m. (b) Intensity at 20 m. (c) Decibel level at 20 m. (d) Distance for 60 dB (threshold of conversation).

Show worked answer

(a) 90 = 10*log(I/10^-12) -> log(I/10^-12) = 9 -> I = 10^-3 W/m^2

(b) Inverse square: I2 = I1*(r1/r2)^2 = 10^-3*(10/20)^2 = 10^-3/4 = 2.5e-4 W/m^2

(c) beta2 = 10*log(2.5e-4/10^-12) = 10*log(2.5e8) = 10*(8+log2.5) = 10*8.4 = 84 dB
    (or: drops by 6 dB when distance doubles: 90-6=84 dB ✓)

(d) 60 dB: I = 10^(6-12) = 10^-6 W/m^2
    I1*r1^2 = I2*r2^2 -> r2 = r1*sqrt(I1/I2) = 10*sqrt(10^-3/10^-6) = 10*sqrt(1000) = 316 m
FRQ 7

Diffraction Grating Analysis

A diffraction grating (500 lines/mm) is used with unknown wavelength light. 2nd order maximum at 35°. (a) Find lambda. (b) Find 1st order angle. (c) Find grating spacing. (d) What is the highest order visible?

Show worked answer

(a) d = 1mm/500 = 2000 nm = 2.0e-6 m
    d*sinθ = m*λ: 2000*sin35° = 2*λ
    λ = 2000*0.574/2 = 574 nm (green-yellow light)

(b) 1st order: d*sin(θ1) = 1*574; sin(θ1) = 574/2000 = 0.287; θ1 = 16.7°

(c) d = 2.0e-6 m = 2 μm = 2000 nm (as calculated)

(d) Max order: d*sin90° = m*λ -> m_max = d/λ = 2000/574 = 3.48 -> m_max = 3
    (4th order would require sinθ > 1, impossible)
FRQ 8

Wave Equation and Superposition

Two waves on same string: y1=0.05 sin(10x - 4t) and y2=0.05 sin(10x + 4t), both in meters. (a) Find A, k, omega, f, v for each. (b) Show they form a standing wave. (c) Find node positions. (d) Find antinode positions and maximum amplitude.

Show worked answer

(a) Both waves: A=0.05m, k=10 rad/m, omega=4 rad/s
    f = omega/(2pi) = 4/(2pi) = 0.637 Hz
    v = omega/k = 4/10 = 0.4 m/s; lambda = 2pi/k = 0.628 m
    y1 travels in +x direction, y2 in -x direction

(b) y_total = y1+y2 = 0.05*sin(10x-4t) + 0.05*sin(10x+4t)
    Using sum-to-product: sin(A-B)+sin(A+B) = 2*sinA*cosB
    y_total = 2*0.05*sin(10x)*cos(4t) = 0.10*sin(10x)*cos(4t)
    This is a standing wave: spatial part [sin(10x)] * temporal part [cos(4t)]

(c) Nodes: sin(10x) = 0 -> 10x = n*pi -> x = n*pi/10 m = n*0.314 m (n=0,1,2,...)

(d) Antinodes: |sin(10x)| = 1 -> 10x = (n+1/2)*pi -> x = (2n+1)*pi/20 m
    Maximum amplitude = 2*A = 0.10 m (at antinodes when |cos(4t)|=1)
FRQ 9

Thin Film Interference

White light hits a 200 nm thick oil film (n=1.5) on water (n=1.33). (a) Phase shifts at each surface. (b) Condition for constructive interference. (c) Which wavelength(s) in visible range (380-700 nm) are strongly reflected?

Show worked answer

(a) Top surface (air n=1 to oil n=1.5): n increases -> PHASE SHIFT (half-lambda shift)
    Bottom surface (oil n=1.5 to water n=1.33): n decreases -> NO phase shift
    Net: ONE phase shift total

(b) With one phase shift: constructive when 2*n*t = (m+1/2)*lambda_air
    2*1.5*200 = 600 nm = (m+1/2)*lambda
    lambda = 600/(m+0.5)
    m=0: lambda=1200 nm (infrared -- not visible)
    m=1: lambda=400 nm (violet edge -- borderline visible)
    m=2: lambda=240 nm (ultraviolet -- not visible)

(c) Strongly reflected: lambda~400 nm (violet, at m=1)
    Other wavelengths not constructively reflected for this thickness.
    The film would appear violet/purple from reflected white light.
    
    For destructive: 2*n*t = m*lambda -> 600 = m*lambda
    m=1: 600 nm (orange-red canceled by destructive interference)
FRQ 10

AP-Style: Wave System Analysis

A speaker (S1, 500 Hz) and another (S2, 500 Hz) are 2.4 m apart, both in phase. v=340 m/s. (a) Find lambda. (b) Find point on the perpendicular bisector between speakers that has first destructive interference. (c) Two speakers now emit 500 Hz and 507 Hz in same room. What happens? (d) If S2 frequency changes to 600 Hz, can you find a point with destructive interference between them? Explain.

Show worked answer

(a) lambda = v/f = 340/500 = 0.68 m

(b) Perpendicular bisector: all points have equal path length from S1 and S2 -> constructive.
    For destructive off the bisector: need path difference = lambda/2 = 0.34 m
    
    Point P on the bisector is at (1.2, y) [midpoint between S1 and S2]:
    Actually, on the perpendicular bisector, path diff = 0 always -> always constructive there.
    First destructive is NOT on the bisector.
    
    Find point where |r1 - r2| = lambda/2 = 0.34 m.
    If point is at distance x along the line joining speakers from midpoint:
    r1 = 1.2+x, r2 = 1.2-x (on the axis between speakers)
    |r1-r2| = 2x = 0.34 -> x = 0.17 m from midpoint
    So: 0.17 m from center on the speaker axis (1.03 m from S1, 1.37 m from S2)

(c) 500 Hz and 507 Hz: beats at 7 Hz. Room fills with sound that pulses 7 times per second -- alternating loud and quiet as the two wave patterns interfere constructively then destructively at each point. Different frequency -> not a simple interference pattern; the pattern changes with time.

(d) 500 Hz and 600 Hz: different frequencies, different wavelengths (0.68 m and 0.567 m).
    The interference pattern shifts constantly because the phase relationship changes with time.
    At any fixed point, the two waves will alternately constructively and destructively interfere -- you'll hear beats at 100 Hz.
    There is NO fixed point of permanent destructive interference; the pattern is time-varying.
    Stable interference (fixed pattern) requires same frequency.
